subtopic: REPORT ON WORK OF SPECIAL SESSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to deal with questions asked me by the hon. member for Queens and the hon. member for Medicine Hat last week concerning the financial situation of the United Nations, and particularly arising out of the problem of the major peace keeping operations of the organization.
These problems have recently been the subject of intensive review by a working group of 21 member states, including Canada. This group was unable, regrettably, to devise an agreed formula for long term financing. Its report suggested elements for an approach which could be adapted to meet the immediate problem of financing these peace keeping operations for the remainder of 1963.
Although other questions such as the payment of arrears and the improvement of budgetary procedures will be considered, the main task of the special assembly of the United Nations is to work out an acceptable method for sharing peace keeping costs on a basis of collective responsibility and a recognition that the less developed countries should be afforded some reduction in their assessments under the regular budgetary scale.
Negotiations to this end are now being vigorously pursued at the United Nations. The Canadian delegation is actually today meeting under its chairmanship with a group of member states to see if some particular formula cannot be devised. The situation is a serious one. The integrity of the United Nations is involved, and Canada is not leaving any effort unexpended in this matter.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed, from Friday, May 24, consideration of the motion of Miss Pauline Jewett for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to the speech from the throne delivered by His Excellency the Administrator at the opening of the session.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
My speech was not intended to be a cliff-hanger or to be delivered in serial form, but in view of the limitation of time on Friday I was obliged to interrupt it. Now I am pleased to deliver part two.
When the house rose on Friday I was speaking about the Atlantic development

board and the government's intention, according to the resolution, to make available $100 million to be divided throughout the tour Atlantic provinces by 11 nominated men. This amounts to $20 million a year for 1964, 1965, 1966, 1967 and 1968, and a question arises regarding the method to be used for the division of this money. What projects will receive priority? Will political considerations supersede economic need? After all, two of the Atlantic provinces have Liberal premiers and two are blessed with Conservative leadership; and the board, with its six additions, will be top heavy with Grits. I sincerely hope the board will give consideration to those projects which will be of benefit to the entire region. We have to do something with this money, little though it may be in relation to the large area to be serviced.
In my opinion the first item for consideration could be the distribution to our universities of some of these development funds. Serving as I do on the board of Waterloo Lutheran University, I am aware of the tremendous growth taking place in this institution in Ontario. Our maritime universities are faced with a similar need for expansion. For example, it is estimated that enrolment at Dalhousie, St. Francis Xavier and Acadia will be doubled within the next ten years. Funds must be found in order to provide the necessary facilities and professors.
We in the Atlantic provinces, and in Nova Scotia in particular, have laboured under a serious disability in connection with the federal university grants program. Because of our high student enrolment in relation to our provincial population, we haye received grants well below the national average. In fact Nova Scotia stands at the bottom of the list, receiving $214 per student last year compared with $495 in Newfoundland and $360 in Ontario. In an age when men are planning a trip to the moon, we have a duty to provide necessary university facilities for our professional, business and political leaders of tomorrow.
A second project I would suggest to the Atlantic development board for consideration concerns the desirability of providing assistance toward establishing an additional ferry service between Nova Scotia and Gloucester, Massachusetts. This would open up a vast potential tourist market, since some 30 million people live in the Gloucester-Boston area. The present ferry, the Bluenose, is unable to handle all the traffic, especially during the peak period from June 1 to September 30. Once these tourists arrive in Nova Scotia they will no doubt wish to visit other Atlantic provinces, and I need not point out the economic benefits that accrue to all our business people from an expanded tourist
The Address-Mr. Crouse industry. It is quite possible they may wish to travel to Newfoundland, to the province of Prince Edward Island or to the province represented so well in this house by the former minister of forestry (Mr. Flemming), the province of New Brunswick. I would urge the government to do everything possible to bring about this worth-while project, bearing in mind that a second ferry service would also provide new outlets and a faster delivery service for our expanding fishing industry.
Speaking of the fishing industry, I note in the speech from the throne that the government is initiating consultation with the provinces to work out a program for national fishery development. Apparently members and supporters of the present government are oblivious to the fact that during the six years when they sat in opposition we brought in a shipbuilding program which is providing new opportunities for our fishermen. The Liberals, when they were previously in office, put into effect a program whereby subsidies were discontinued in respect of ships over 65 feet in length. Unlike them, we instituted a policy whereby a federal subsidy is paid on ships of any length of over 45 feet. As a result our shipyards are booming from Cape Breton to Yarmouth. In my riding the shipbuilding yards in Mahone Bay, Lunenburg and Dayspring have a year's work booked ahead, while at Liverpool, Nova Scotia, a steel ship is under construction for the first time in history, all as a result of the constructive and far reaching policies worked out and put into operation by a Conservative government. These ships are all of a size which will assure greater safety to our fishermen while assisting them to earn larger incomes. I only wish the former prime minister, the present Leader of the Opposition, could visit Nova Scotia to see the beneficial effects of his shipbuilding program. However, we welcome any program which will be of benefit to our fishing industry, and I will watch with interest the program to be put forward by the present administration.
In the speech from the throne there is a statement indicating that the government intends to establish a 12-mile limit for the benefit of Canadian fishermen. All of us from the Atlantic provinces are interested in the fishing industry in one way or another, and I have placed a resolution on the order paper asking the present government to take immediate action to conserve our marine fishery resources by declaring certain bodies of water adjacent to our coast Canadian national waters. I have suggested that the straight base line method be used to measure the breadth of territorial seas, and that recognition be given by Canada to the historic

The Address-Mr. Crouse fishing rights of France and the United States in Canadian national waters.
This is in keeping with the views I expressed in the house when speaking on the Coastal Fisheries Protection Act on January 30, 1962. A base line drawn from Grand Manan to cape Fourchu would seal off the bay of Fundy, while a base line drawn from cape Sable to Scatari island would seal off St. Margaret bay and Chedabucto bay. A line drawn from cape North to Port aux Basques, Newfoundland, would seal off the gulf of St. Lawrence, and this would then become a territorial sea wherein conservation measures could be carried out on the vast Bradelle bank and Orphan bank.
This action will not solve all our problems, but the rapid increase in world fishing effort and efficiency and the terrific concentration of foreign trawlers off our coast have focused attention on the fact that unless some safeguards are taken the marine resources that have played such a vital role in the development of the Canadian economy will be harvested by foreign fleets. However, in my opinion France and the United States should be given historic rights in Canadian national waters. France owns the islands of St. Pierre and Miquelon, and along with the United States has historic rights under the treaty of Utrecht of 1713 modified by the convention of 1904 and the treaty of London of 1818. Nations not having historic fishing rights with Canada should be denied access to our marine resources within the areas enclosed by the proposed base line.
I am concerned, however, by a statement made by the present Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill). Speaking during the recent election campaign at Sydney, Nova Scotia he said:
Under a Liberal government foreign fishing ships would not be permitted within the 12-mile limit.
This is reported in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald.
Mr. Pickersgill, in a quick swing through Cape Breton, said Liberals would call a federal-provincial conference on the fish business. "We are not going to beat around the bush about the 12-mile limit.' He said if other nations would not go along "we will do it alone."
The present Prime Minister, also speaking at Sydney, said:
Because an agreement of a 12-mile limit had not been reached, X think the time has now come for such unilateral action. I am sure that if Norway and Iceland can do this, so can we in a way which will not cause difficulties with our friends.
That, Mr. Speaker, is exactly what we are hoping to prevent, namely difficulties with our friends. We do not want a gunboat fisheries policy in the Atlantic provinces similar to the gunboat policy of Iceland in

September, 1958. The export of Canadian fisheries products reached a record in 1962 of $156,615,000, an increase of 9 per cent over 1961. We are the third largest fish exporting nation in the world, and we rank seventh among the fish producing nations. More than 79,000 Canadians are commercial fishermen and, just for the record, the United States imports approximately 70 per cent of Canada's total fish exports. I need not point out to the house the economic havoc that the loss of this market would create in the Atlantic provinces as the result of any rash or hasty action on the part of the present administration.
According to the press, President Kennedy continues to favour the three-mile territorial and fisheries limit. If this is so, we in the Atlantic provinces want to know. We have a right to know, for our very livelihood is at stake, about the government's negotiations with the United States on a 12-mile fishing limit. I believe this 12-mile limit can only be established through international agreement and by giving American fishermen equal rights with Canadian fishermen, thereby assuring continuing friendly relations between our two countries and the continuing expansion of the market for our fishery products.
The United States fishing industry is highly organized. They have the national fisheries institute in Washington as well as an organization called the New Bedford seafood council. With the rapid expansion of our ground-fish industry and our scallop industry, we must have continuing free access to the United States market if we are to avoid a serious marketing problem in the Atlantic provinces. We need to start some measures of conservation such as I have outlined, but we must also maintain our markets, and I cannot urge too strongly upon the present administration the necessity of attaining both these objectives.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like first of all to take this opportunity of offering you the customary congratulations upon your appointment to the position of Speaker of this house. I should like to add another motive for these congratulations: there exists now in the house an atmosphere of freedom that we had not known for at least a year. However, I must assure you of our co-operation, for freedom of speech does not necessarily mean libertinism.
Mr. Speaker, since the last session, there was a general election and once more the people again had to choose their representatives in the house. There have been few

changes. Two political parties have changed sides in the house, but since then, I believe that their speeches, whether they sit on the right or on the left, are strangely similar. The members of the present opposition claim that everything was fine when they were in power and those who are presently in power say that they form the best government Canada has ever had, or exactly the opposite of what was taking place last year.
Mr. Speaker, the last election taught us a lesson. Money has been spent during the last campaign, and a kind of brainwashing was performed on a large scale throughout the country. But, in spite of everything, it was apparent that, during the last election, the voters did not fall as they have in the past, for these brainwashing techniques accompanied by high sounding publicity, as well as by heavy expenditures. The Quebec population had enough judgment to give more than 600,000 votes, or 30 per cent of the total in the province of Quebec to a middle party, that is to say the Social Credit party, which carried out its campaign with very little money, relying mostly on the dedication of its benevolent organizers. I believe that the province of Quebec would have sent to Ottawa a majority of Social Credit members had 10 or 12 per cent more voters supported us.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take this opportunity to pay a well-deserved tribute to two persons who have spread wholesome ideas and done a task of political, social and economical education throughout the country. I am thinking, first of all, of our national leader, the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), who did not make any false promise, but who was content with putting forward ideas to the Canadian population, explaining the problems that we have to face today. He did not roam about the country decrying people or seeking to prejudice reputations or to spread falsehoods throughout the country. Rather, he tried to propose a solution, a monetary system which would give a new expansion to the Canadian economy, an expansion which the country can enjoy and which it deserves at present.
In second place, I should like to address my congratulations to our national assistant leader, the hon. member for Villeneuve (Mr. Caouette) for the manner in which he conducted the election campaign in the province of Quebec. It was also a clean campaign; he outlined ideas and tried to appeal to the common sense of the people, rather than to their lowest instincts.
The Address-Mr. Gregoire
Mr. Speaker, perhaps the speech from the throne that we have before us is somewhat vague, but I suggest that it is like all the other speeches from the throne. It gives indications that there might be some achievements from the legislation that the government will bring forward. Let us hope that the attitude of the government in this field will differ from that it seems to take in the case of the matters that we had been putting forward since the beginning of the session. We get vague replies, or rather, no replies at all. When we put a question to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), his favourite answers can be summed up in the following manner: "We shall give you a reply in due time. We shall take care of that a little later. We cannot make an announcement right now".
Their answers are most evasive and I hope that in the future members of the cabinet can be more factual and give us the answers we expect to get.
Mr. Speaker, the most serious problem today is still the economic situation. Our people live in a condition of prevailing economic stagnation. In fact, unemployment is developing at a rate a little too high for a country such as Canada. We note that industry finds it difficult to develop, that it cannot advance. At the same time, trade is declining.
We must get our economy moving again and provide for its expansion.
The speech from the throne announced measures aimed at giving expansion to our Canadian economy but it does not contain a paragraph that we find in the Liberal party platform for the 1963 general election. In fact, I have that platform in my hand and on page 11 I find a paragraph which does not appear in the speech from the throne but which would have opened the door to all the solutions that the speech from the throne would like to apply. I think that paragraph is more important than all the rest of the Liberal party policy and even more important than the speech from the throne itself. I quote:
A new Liberal government will see to it that the money supply is large enough to insure that tight money will not paralyse business-
A new Liberal government will see to it that the money supply is large enough-
Mr. Speaker, I feel that the major problem facing Canada at this time is that of the money supply. Our country's possibilities are out of proportion with the amount of currency in circulation.

The Address-Mr. Gregoire
It is proposed to help create new industries at a time when existing industries are marking time and several of them have to close down or reduce production. Why is that? Because the available money supply is not sufficient for Canadian consumers to purchase all our production.
And by Canadian consumers, I mean the federal government, the provincial governments, the municipalities and the school boards as well as the individuals.
This morning questions were addressed to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier) about construction of penitentiaries. Everybody in this house will agree that there is a scarcity of penitentiaries, but the Minister of Justice stated: "We cannot build any because our budget does not enable us to". So this is a matter of budget not a matter of our country's productive capacity.
People ask for the erection of post offices. The erection of those buildings is acknowledged to be imperative, but our budget is such that we cannot afford it.
For many long years, the voters in my riding have requested the erection of an armoury building. It will not be built because our budget does not allow it.
Yet the capacity for building those structures is there. But the money supply, the credit which would enable us to erect those buildings and thus reduce unemployment, is not there. Why? Simply because the government has no control over the money supply, over the credit which would enable this country to expand.
The present Liberal administration is fully aware of that because they said in their program:
A new Liberal government will see to it that the money supply is large enough to ensure that tight money will not paralyse business-
And it is precisely a tight money situation which is paralysing business today.
Consider for instance the government of the province of Quebec facing all sorts of difficulties because they do not have available to them the credit that would be necessary for a full expansion of industry, as well as of the education, health and highway facilities. Since they do not have the necessary credit, the government of the province of Quebec are now serving an ultimatum-this is the word used by the premier of the province of Quebec himself-asking a better tax-sharing arrangement from the federal government in order

that the provinces may develop by themselves, and this ultimatum from the province of Quebec is based on the need to obtain new credit to successfully implement their program, because the province of Quebec has roads to build but no money to do it.
On the other hand, the federal government are in a sort of disastrous situation. They find themselves in hot water because this request comes from one of the main supporters of the federal Liberal party in the last general election, none other than the premier of the province of Quebec.
But, the present administration know very well that they cannot return to the province its sources of revenue because they are themselves in a disastrous financial situation at the present time and they must face unbalanced budgeting and accumulated deficits. This government must face the problem of health insurance and they must replenish the unemployment insurance fund. How can we expect the federal government to do away with its sources of revenue when it needs them itself.
We can feel at the present time that there is dissension between the two levels of government and it is due not only to the fact that the money is not there for those who need it but also that the governments try to grab for themselves the little there is. In fact, it is as if there were on a plate a single piece of pie over which the federal government and the provincial governments were fighting.
The best suggestion we can make to the government at the present time is to read over carefully that section on page 11 of the Liberal platform for the 1963 general election. If the government applied that section, it would realize that all the other pledges that they made or which are contained in that booklet can be readily implemented.
In fact, this booklet contains statements concerning old age pensions and assistance for the construction of houses. But nothing can be done now because, as it happens, no money is available for that purpose.
I wish to point out to the house many problems which are ignored in our country at the present time, especially the role assigned to the industrial development bank. That institution was established to help the existing small industries, but it now refuses about 90 per cent of the loans' applications,

precisely because it does not have the necessary money to help small industry to develop. There is no co-ordination between the various departments who could help to solve the industry's problems. In this connection, I should like to mention a striking example of what took place in my riding.
Some time ago, that is immediately after the holiday period, a manufacturer in my riding, who owned a small mattress industry, was hiring ten employees at the time, but had orders on hand which exceeded ten times the number of mattresses he was able to put out, i.e., from 800 to 900 mattresses a year. Now, I accompanied that business man who wanted to obtain a loan from the industrial development bank. After having submitted his request, he was told: "We cannot grant you a loan, your business is not large enough." Now, mind you, Mr. Speaker, this man is anxious to enlarge his business, and it was for that very purpose that he was asking for a loan of $40,000, which would have enabled him to hire 50 new employees, and to reduce the number of Canadian unemployed proportionately, and more particularly in my riding.
After he had exhausted all arguments, I said to the manager. "But if you grant him a loan of $40,000, this means that there will be 50 fewer unemployed in the county of Jon-quiere, who will then have no need for social benefits or unemployment insurance payments-each of them receives an average of $100 a month in unemployment insurance benefits. This would therefore, mean a saving of $60,000 a year for the unemployment insurance fund, for this is the amount now paid in benefits to the 50 unemployed who would then have found work. If the government had granted a loan of $40,000 to this small business man, it would, in a year, have saved $60,000 for the unemployment insurance fund; moreover the federal government would receive taxes from those former unemployed who would be working and realize a profit even if the loan were not immediately repaid.
But the manager answered: "I understand those needs very well; however, this is no concern of mine. It comes under the unemployment insurance branch."
And if you try to explain that problem to the unemployment insurance commission officials, they will not understand it either.
As you see, Mr. Speaker, there is no coordination between the various government 28902-5-20
The Address-Mr. Gregoire departments. The unemployment insurance commission is interested only in paying allowances to the unemployed, without requiring the latter to work. On the other hand the industrial development bank is not interested at all in helping reduce unemployment in Canada.
Rather than keep on creating a lot of boards, economic councils and so on, the services of all government departments should be co-ordinated in order that the taxpayers' money be spent wisely.
Mr. Speaker, last year, amendments were made by this house to the federal Farm Credit Corporation Act, so that farmers of the province of Quebec, like those of eastern Canada, could derive greater profit from it. We hoped it would be a good piece of legislation.
Well, in my riding, hundreds of requests were made, but barely 2 per cent were accepted.
Legislation is adopted to help the farmer, but when the farmer asks for any assistance, it is refused, so that the act becomes almost inoperative. What good is it then to pass legislation in this House of Commons if it is not put to some use, and inspectors or managers in the various government departments see to it that it is not.
Mr. Speaker, I would now like to deal with another problem. There has been talk in the house lately about problems raised by the coexistence of the two great nations making up our country. Mention is made of the establishment of a royal commission on bicul-turalism or the study of that problem.
I read in a newspaper this morning that a government member has made a suggestion which I feel is very sensible. He said: "In the forthcoming days and months, we should concentrate in obtaining bilingualism in the federal civil service without further delay." And the member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Pepin) expresses fear that the holding of a royal commission on biculturalism might well lead French Canada to miss the boat once again.
It is a fact, Mr. Speaker, that because of the delays which will ensue from the inquiry, we may lose sight of our objective. As the hon. member for iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Sauve) stated the other day, there are many things which should be improved in our own house; the structures of the federal government, of parliament itself, should be revised. Even in the parliament buildings, in Ottawa, there are serious gaps as far as bilingualism is concerned.

The Address-Mr. Gregoire
In my opinion, the present government should not wait until the royal commission on biculturalism submits a report to put its own house in order. It should ensure that throughout Canada, full recognition is given to bilingualism not only in all fields pertaining to federal jurisdiction but also in matters which come under the provinces. Lately I received two pamphlets. One is a C.N.R. publication called "C.N. Keeps Track" which deals with a certain number of promotions. That was the issue of May 1963, written in English. Out of 24 promotions given lately at the C.N.R., only three went to French Canadians. That is what is happening in May 1963, only five or six months after the repentant president of the C.N.R. assured us that there would be no recurrence of such situations.
I have also before me the Canadian Travel News, written in English.
(Text):
T.C.A. holds staff Instructional courses for personnel.
(Translation):
Courses, that is, to prepare its personnel for promotions. Out of the 29 employees who follow those courses there is not a single French Canadian.
It is my contention, sir, that the government should look more closely into the matter; it should institute reforms right now instead of waiting for the establishment of a commission of inquiry.
But I think that a still more serious problem exists. Language is not the only difficulty in Canada today. My grandfather and my father spoke French in the province of Quebec; I speak French and my seven-year-old son speaks French very well. I am convinced that we will keep on speaking our language, and we have proved it for 200 years.
However, the heart of the problem lies somewhere else. It is rather that at the present time, among French speaking Canadians, especially in the province of Quebec, the idea of "decolonization" is spreading, as it is throughout the world, but in our province it is more a matter of "economic decolonization".
We feel that, in the economic field, Canadians from coast to coast are more or less "economically colonized" by foreign countries. We do not control our own economy. We do not control our own industry. And the French

Canadians, feeling this much more deeply than the English Canadians at the present time- I am sure of that-would like to break those chains, those economic ties that bind us too closely to other countries.
Now, in this economic decolonization effort the French Canadians lack the support of the English Canadians to walk in line with them. They feel that, in this decolonization effort, they have to drag the English Canadians along with them, and the burden they have to carry becomes too heavy. They say: we might as well go it alone and let the other provinces sink into foreign economic control, if that is what they wish.
Proofs of this are to be seen everywhere. A few days ago, I received-and all hon. members must have received it too-a report on small loan companies from the superintendent of insurance for Canada. I always go through these reports for I find them interesting. For instance, take the two largest of these small finance companies operating in Canada. The largest one, Beneficial Finance Company of Canada, has an authorized and issued capital of $10 million. Out of these $10 million, $9,980,000 have been issued to Beneficial Finance Company of Wilmington, Delaware, U.S.A., and only $20,000 were issued to Canadians. Twenty thousand dollars, out of $10 million, were issued to Canadians and $9,980,000 to an American company. Last year, with this authorized and issued capital of $10 million, this company had a surplus of $9,188,738.01. Making $9,188,000 with an authorized capital of $10 million is what I would call a paying proposition. But profits do not go to Canadians; they go to an American company that comes here to get our money. This is what I feel is important: they come in our country to get our money.
The second finance company mentioned in the report, Household Finance Corporation of Canada, has an authorized capital of $5 million, but with $3,075,000 issued and paid up. The president, Mr. F. A. McDonald of Chicago, Illinois, has subscribed $3,052,000 out of $3,075,000 which leaves about $17,000 subscribed by Canadians. That gives you an idea of the situation, Mr. Speaker.
And you can look into all the other branches of our economy. Not so long ago, two important Canadian chartered banks, the Imperial Bank of Canada and the Canadian Bank of Commerce, merged under the name

of the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce. According to the Canada Gazette a British bank is the major stockholder in the merger.
Foreign capital controls our economy in such sectors as financial companies, industrial concerns, banks and many others. From the economic viewpoint, Canada is a colony, under the control of foreign enterprises, and our country has become a sort of private hunting ground, where these enterprises become rich at our expense.
In the field of insurance, how many Canadian companies sell insurance in France, Great Britain, the United States or Belgium? On the other hand, innumerable foreign insurance companies come over here, collect Canadian money and pocket their profits. The same situation prevails in all other areas.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I say that we feel we are not the masters of our own country. And industry in the province of Quebec does not belong to English speaking Canadians.
No, it is not the citizens in the province of Ontario who are to blame if we are not masters of our own industries in our province of Quebec. It is rather the result of a whole set of circumstances if our industries today are owned, not by Canadians but by foreigners.
Like the citizens of other countries who in the last few years, had felt the same need, the French Canadian people want to throw off the foreign yoke. If they cannot get the co-operation and collaboration of the English speaking Canadians in order to share in this struggle for economic liberation and that of their province, then the French Canadians are prepared to go ahead alone, because the Canadians from the other parts of the country do not seem ready to participate in the same effort in order to free themselves from the economic foreign hold which controls our economy today.
Mr. Speaker, I think that it is a very sensible feeling.
How is it that every year our minister of finance tells us: "We have a tremendous trade deficit". Last year, in reply to a question, the then minister of finance, who is now in the opposition, said this:
There was an outflow of $1,100 million in Canadian money last year in payment of dividends, interest and profits to foreign companies operating our Canadian industries.

It is obvious, Mr. Speaker, because while Canadian labour unions in the nine other provinces are all branches of international unions, in the province of Quebec we have a Canadian union, the confederation of labour unions, which is the only important independent union in the province of Quebec and in all Canada.
Even the labour leaders in the other provinces accept such a situation, that is being under the control of international unions. It is amazing, all the same, to find that money is leaving Canada under the form of labour contributions paid to international labour unions. It is amazing also that English speaking workers do not realize that they are themselves under the economic domination of foreigners.
I am sure our workers in Quebec are intelligent enough to look after their own. They have set up their own trade unions, like the C.S.N., which is in a much better position today than the unions which have to take orders from outside.
I have touched upon only a few points relating to finance companies, trade unions and Canadian industries. However, I could give many other instances.
If we wish to realize national unity, we will have to get together and become masters in our own house.
Mr. Speaker, we do not even have a distinctive Canadian flag. Is that not a sufficient proof of our immaturity? How then can we hope to shake off the last remnants of foreign political domination? But such is indeed our present state of mind.
Some of my constituents sometimes tell me: "We have the Queen's picture on our dollar bills; does it mean that if these dollars are scarce, it is because the Queen of England does not wish to give us more?"
Mr. Speaker, French Canadians want to throw off the last traces of foreign sway. Their claim appears to be just and reasonable. I think, as they do, that if all Canadians throughout the country worked together to abolish foreign control of their economy, they would be masters in their own home, freed from the control of foreign enterprises whose head offices are on foreign soil.
A truly Canadian flag is naturally very important, but not quite as important as to be master of one's own castle. Perhaps the

The Address-Mr. Mather English speaking Canadians are not too concerned about their freedom, but French Canadians are very attached to it. If the English speaking provinces do not wish to help us to free ourselves in every respect, we would be ready to mark off the boundaries of our own province.
When we are promised a flag within two years, I cannot but recall that the French Canadians had to fight for 20 years in order to obtain at last bilingual cheques and the right to conduct bank transactions in both languages. The former minister of finance settled the matter in five seconds. He merely said to the printer: "Print the cheques in both languages".
The same thing should be done as regards the choice of a flag. The question would be settled as quickly as the other one if the Prime Minister just gave to the employee appointed to hoist the flag on the parliament buildings the order to hoist some distinctive national flag, whatever its design. It is useless to spend two years trying to find a proper design, for there will always be people who are not satisfied. There are 4,000 designs of flags at present in the files of the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill). However, it would be possible to select a distinctive flag within the space of ten seconds.
You may find I am simplifying the problem. In fact, it has to be simplified if it is to be settled. The important thing is to be free from all traces of ties and domination such as we have had in the past.
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that all the problems Canada now has to face in the economic field can be solved.
I have mentioned but one point taken in a brief paragraph of the Liberal program. I do not wish to be unduly critical of the new government, for I do want it to prove itself, especially concerning the questions I raised earlier.
I shall end here, since my time has expired. Let the suggestion contained in this short paragraph be put in practice, and many problems will be solved, which is what all Canadians wish. Then we shall reach a lasting understanding in our country.

Mr. Speaker, the compliments which previous speakers have paid to yourself and your deputy on your appointments have been so well worded that I think it unnecessary for me to further take up the time of the house by repeating them. However, I would like to say just this, that in my opinion if the government only shows the same good judgment

in other matters during this session as it did in your appointments, the work and responsibility of the opposition would be very greatly reduced.
Mr. Speaker, I come from the riding of New Westminster, which is the deep southwest of Canada. This riding has more people in it than has the province of Prince Edward Island. It is the largest riding, as regards population, west of Toronto. As I say, we have more people in our riding than there are in the province of Prince Edward Island. That province, however, as you know, has at all times four members in this house and four members in the other place, whereas our riding of New Westminster, with its larger population, has only Senator Reid and myself to carry on all its work. So you can see how busy we must be, sir.
In many respects New Westminster is, I think, a good cross section representation of many other ridings of Canada. We have many large developments in agriculture, dairying, fruit and vegetable growing. We have a large fishing fleet based there, many lumbering and saw mill operations, plus a growing number of secondary industrial manufacturing concerns. In addition, many people who work in the larger city of Vancouver make their home in the three municipalities and three cities of New Westminster riding.
I think the people who live in our riding are very much like the people who reside in other parts of Canada. They have the same basic needs. They want health, education, employment and peace. They have sent me here again, sir, to do what I can to get these elementary things for them and make them possible for their children. In my view I can only succeed to the degree that this nation, and indeed the whole world, proceeds on the basis of planning and co-operation for the welfare of the majority.
Mr. Speaker, we in the New Democratic party have very little hope of the present administration achieving very much along that line. As the previous prime minister said, I think last session, "We hope but with little hope". We know, like the official opposition whose members are mostly still dedicated to the ideals of outmoded laissez faire capitalism, that the government has the same general ideas, and that it has only reluctantly and out of economic necessity begun to speak now of economic planning and collective collaboration. We know there are serious omissions in the throne speech. There are many subjects which have not been gone into. For example, I think a very serious problem in this country which we should face up to is the fact that we are spending something like 40

cents of each federal tax dollar on the nonconstructive items of armaments and debt interest. Can we afford to do this?
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, our party sees in the throne speech, after all these years, a few of the things which we in this party, and in the C.C.F. before us and in the Progressives before them, a few of the things which we worked to bring about. We see that the throne speech promises action on planning and on economic boards for the better production and distribution of goods and services. Second, we welcome in the throne speech an intimation that there is to be a beginning of contributory pensions and an increase in the present pension. We hope again that these matters will be undertaken in very short order, and that it will not be proved to be a move which will be too little and too late. It might be considered that for the past 15 or 20 years in this country approximately 25 per cent of the value of pensions has been consumed by the constant inflation which has taken place over that period.
The subject of redistribution is mentioned in the throne speech, and we are all for that. There is a pressing need for Canada to redress the present unfair basis of representation in parliament which gives such legislative power into the hands of rural minorities. As you know, in the United States citizens in urban and suburban communities have recently taken action in the courts to secure a better form of representation for themselves in the councils of their nation. In Canada, Mr. Speaker, we in the New Democratic party have consistently polled over one million votes, which should entitle us on a numerical basis to something like 35 to 40 seats in this house. Yet the system of representation which we have-or should I say "misrepresentation"-limits us to about half that number. We are glad to see that the government intends to redistribute our electoral units. We would also favour action to bring in absentee voting. At the present time scores of thousands of industrial workers are disfranchised at every election.
The 12-mile fishing limit is also mentioned in the throne speech and is a matter which has been fought for by those of us in this part of the house for many years. Indeed, I have a bill calling for the 12-mile limit on the order paper at this time, and I had it there last session. While I am not from Missouri but from British Columbia, where the people long ago learned to distinguish between promises and performances, I intend to leave my bill on the order paper until I see the legislation the government is speaking of bringing in.
Mr. Speaker, we in this part of the house consider that our function is not to block but
The Address-Mr. Mather to push, not to drag but to drive, not to slow down but to speed up. We in this party are here to oppose delay. We are not here to defeat this government; we are here to get the best and quickest possible results for the people of Canada. But, Mr. Speaker, we can do little or nothing to achieve a better Canada unless or until we have a better world. We have some terrible contrasts and maladjustments in our present world. It is a very small world now; we can fly around it in minutes and send messages around it in seconds. We are now trying to get to other worlds and will very likely succeed, unless in the meantime we succeed in blowing up and destroying our present world. At the same time over half the people in the world are said to go to bed hungry at night. Millions are suffering from disease. Hundreds of millions cannot communicate with each other, cannot read or write.
For our part, we in this part of the world have to deal not with shortages but with surpluses. It strikes me that nearly all the problems which come before us in this house arise from problems of surpluses, having their roots in production or in the deployment of our manpower. Our problem is one of distributing the vast wealth which we have produced, and this is an impossibility under private enterprise alone. These are some of the problems and maladjustments which exist.
Mankind is further divided by our political creeds. We here call for increased support of United Nations agencies, and we mean to exert every effort we can to see that this is done. In my view, Mr. Speaker, the first essential is to work for peace. Without that we have nothing. In that connection I should like to compliment the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) on her recognition of the changes which are taking place in the international scene and for what I took to be her personal opinion that the time is drawing near when this country should recognize China.
Mr. Speaker, in that regard I have a proposal to make to the government. If we can have two ministers of agriculture, could we not have two ministers of external affairs? It seems to me that if the government would appoint the hon. member for Northumberland as the minister of external affairs for the Pacific region it would be a very good thing. I can promise her the warmest support from this quarter of the house.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is well for us at this time to consider the historical fact that the differences that we in the western world have with those of the east, considering all the divisions and the bitterness existing

The Address-Mr. Mather between us, are yet less than those which a few centuries ago plunged the world into religious wars which plagued Europe for centuries. As someone has written, if those who had been involved in the religious wars of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries could return to earth today, they would be astonished to find the old hatreds gone and that the old antagonists, instead of burning each other at the stake, are able to live together peaceably and discuss things in a rational manner.
I should like to urge upon the government, and particularly on the Prime Minister, that they do not isolate Canada or lessen her power for peace by perpetually and automatically turning a deaf ear and a blind eye, as some do, to offers or actions of a conciliatory nature which may be made by the other side. We on our side of this world dispute are not all white, and those on the other side are not all black. I think there is meaning in the words of the former president of the United States, President Eisenhower, when he said that the people of the world want peace so much that unless their leaders get it for them they will somehow push them out of the way and unite for peace of their own accord.
Mr. Speaker, our Prime Minister has recently visited the United States. I understand that he intends to go again. Still more recently we have had the NATO conference here. I suggest to the Prime Minister that he consider-perhaps he has already done so- the possibility of making a visit to Russia to see if he cannot use some of those powers of his which once won him the peace prize of the world toward securing at least a better feeling and an easing of tensions between that country and our neighbour to the south. We would have nothing to lose by this. Ultimately we are either going to live together or die together; there is no other alternative.
Turning now to our internal affairs, I should like to put forward a few of my own proposals. One of the growing services of our nation is transportation. It is something which affects us all. I think a great deal more federal attention should be given to transportation; because whether it be air, sea, train or bus, transportation is now subsidized by the taxpayer. In many instances a subsidized part of the industry is competing on its subsidy with another subsidized part of the industry. I believe the time is here when we should set up a comprehensive, all-embracing transportation authority in Canada which will have power to plan and regulate the expenditure of public money on

transportation, so that the best result could be achieved for all and particularly for the public.
Another point I should like to put forward is that there is a need for a very much stepped up and more imaginative program for our rapidly approaching centennial celebrations. These take place, Mr. Speaker, in 1967, and speaking as one who had something to do with the initiation and organization of the 1958 centennial celebrations in British Columbia, I think it should be pointed out that we are behind time with our national celebration preparations. These will take place in 1967, and plans for them must be completed by the end of 1966. We are now almost half way through 1963, so there are approximately 43 months left to prepare for these celebrations and ensure that they are of the magnitude which a country of Canada's size should expect.
We still seem to be lagging. Is it because we have not got the right kind of organization? Is it because we are not providing enough money? Is it because we lack the imagination to see what this birthday celebration can do for Canada at home and abroad? For one thing, I would like to think that on the morning of January 1, 1967 not only across Canada but around the world the new flag of Canada, which the government promises, should be unfurled in simultaneous demonstration.
An additional proposal I want to make concerns taxation. In the United States municipal taxes and mortgage interest payments on homes are deductible from federal taxes. They should be here, too. This would encourage home building, home owning and family stability, to say nothing of stimulating increased business in the construction industry and in all the many related businesses.
Second, I call for the levying of a capital gains tax on stock market profits. Canada is one of the very few countries which does not have such a tax. Millions could be secured from it and put to work to reduce either the public debt or the level of other taxation.
In the field of citizenship and unity, I feel that whether we are English speaking Canadians, French speaking Canadians or members of that other great group, the new Canadians, the important thing is that we are Canadians. In this connection I make a modest suggestion. We use the translation hearing aids, but for the people who visit us and sit in the galleries there are no such aids. If they are English speaking Canadians, without French, they must listen to 20 minutes of oratory of which they can understand nothing. If they are French speaking Canadians without English, they must hear a speech in

English, such as my own, without comprehending any of it. I think it only right that we should install in the galleries translation hearing aids which would enable our visitors to tune in on all of us. And when they do so they will find, I am sure, that though we are speaking in different ways, in our ideas we speak the same language. I put forward as a serious suggestion the provision of translation hearing aids for the galleries.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, there are the local issues or problems of my own constituency. I hope this new government will go ahead at once with matters which have been on the books, so to speak, for years, including the reorganization of the present New Westminster port authority into an enlarged Fraser river authority, giving representation to the municipalities along the banks of that great stream. I will have more to say on these and other matters as we progress in this session. I resume my seat now so that other members will have an opportunity to speak.

Mr. Speaker, on May 16 I took my seat for the first time in this House of Commons as one of the elected members from the dual constituency of Halifax. It is a constituency in which 225,000 Nova Scotians reside.
Within its boundaries are two cities; Halifax, the historic capital of Nova Scotia, and Dartmouth, one of the most rapidly expanding cities in Canada. Outside its urban area it includes the beautiful farming district of the Musquodoboit valley. Along its Atlantic coast boundary are found picturesque fishing villages such as Peggy's Cove, Little Harbour and many others, the home of the hardy inshore fishermen, unique places of interest to artists, relaxing vacation spots for those who enjoy Nova Scotia's rugged coast line.
My constituency includes that world famous east coast port from which convoys sailed during both world wars to maintain vital supply line to the allied forces overseas. The port of Halifax, one of Canada's year round ice free Atlantic ocean ports, is a major base for Canada's armed forces. Around its shores are found nationally recognized universities and colleges-Dalhousie, St. Mary's, Kings and Pine Hill-as well as the offices of departments and crown corporations of this federal government. For example, there are armed forces establishments, the national harbours board, the Bedford institute of oceanography, C.N.R., T.C.A., central mortgage and housing, the Department of National Revenue and the Bank of Canada.
The extensive facilities of the Halifax shipyards, including floating and dry docks for
The Address-Mr. Lloyd new ship construction and ship repairs, provide a key industry. Expanding oil refineries and secondary manufacturing plants are located on the Dartmouth side of the harbour. In short, my constituency is a metropolitan urban growth area, the seat of provincial government and a centre of banking, trade and commerce. According to economic base and other studies, the population could rise to 300,000 in the next ten to 15 years.
For many years I have enjoyed the privilege of service in the Halifax city council, and was its mayor when elected to this house. I am most pleased to have associated with me, as a Liberal member from our dual constituency, a young energetic member of the bar of Nova Scotia. He has to his credit many accomplishments in the field of labour management relations.
My colleague has brought to your attention the serious threat to the volume of winter port traffic at Halifax with advent of extensive icebreaker operations in the upper reaches of the St. Lawrence. We shall seek the co-operation of the government and this house to adopt constructive proposals that will stop the gradual erosion of our winter port business, a vital and substantial element in the economic base of the port region around Halifax harbour.
We shall also seek the co-operation of the government and parliament in correcting a serious injustice in the policy of grants in lieu of municipal taxation of crown properties. For example, in Montreal-and I should like my colleagues from Quebec to note this-the C.N.R. is liable for, and pays to that city, 100 per cent of municipal real property taxes, business taxes and water taxes. In Halifax a privy council order limits such grants to 50 per cent of the real property tax. The Nova Scotian hotel enjoys a ten year tax agreement limiting its tax payment to $60,000 per year. In the city of Montreal the Queen Elizabeth hotel is liable for 100 per cent of all city taxes. For 1963 that tax bill ran close to $1 million.
The national harbours board grants in lieu of taxation are confined to the equivalent of rated police and fire protection taxation on its properties throughout Canada. The board contends its operating deficits prohibit it from meeting the liability for grants equal to 100 per cent of real property taxation. On the other hand, like the C.N.R. the national harbours board continues to accumulate interest charges on outstanding loans and advances from the national treasury, its only source of capital funds. Only part of that interest accrual is actually paid. Its 1962 balance sheet shows $71,290,474 in interest arrears. It also continues to make provision for depreciation of its fixed assets. At December 31, 1962, it

The Address-Mr. Lloyd held approximately $60 million in treasury bills and government bonds tor replacement of capital assets.
The board has been unable to supply us with any consistent definitive policy with respect to the disposal of replacement reserve funds. In fact they have been employed as working capital funds. In short, the board's contention that it cannot afford to meet local taxation is indefensible. Grants in lieu of taxation on crown property do more than relieve the pressure on the local ratepayer. They provide an import dollar quotient to our port region, with its beneficial multiplier effects in our marginal economy.
Until we improve on our present office arrangement, my colleague and I run the risk of being distinguished in this house as the centre block speaking and the west block speaking members for Halifax. With that temporary disability overcome, we look forward to more effective teamwork in this house. Despite our professional backgrounds, we readily admit our need for experience with the unfamiliar procedural rules and the general modus operandi of this national parliament. During orientation to my duties I have gone through the usual initial periods of frustration and bewilderment that confront all new members. Setting up a small office in share quarters is an example. I share with the hon. member for Kings (Mr. Mul-lally) a splendid view of the excellent masonry at the back of the peace tower. On the other hand, I have enjoyed many moments of enlightenment afforded to me by understanding, co-operative and experienced hon. members and civil staff members.
Despite that willing co-operation, for which I am most grateful, I have continued in orbit around Ottawa to such an extent that I believe I vie with the accomplishment of astronaut Cooper. At this moment, my first speech in this house, I begin the re-entry program, with procedural controls in your hands, Mr. Speaker. I trust that I shall successfully land on my feet from cloud nine without unscheduled stops on the clouds in between. Now I turn to my re-entry rockets.
I share with all hon. members, Mr. Speaker, a deep sense of appreciation that you were available and willing, with the customary display of traditional reluctance, to undertake the onerous duties of Speaker. Your wide experience and highly respected service as a member of previous parliaments should greatly expedite the urgent work to be performed by this house.
I now turn to my specific comments on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. The right hon. leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) spoke in derogatory terms of the decisions made by the new


Liberal ministry. It is my purpose to show that the right hon. member has made assertions about the throne speech that are unsupported by any foundation in fact. Indeed, the right hon. member in his former capacity as prime minister of Canada is now on the opposite side of the house because he failed to make the very decisions Canadians urgently needed and wanted and which are now the decisions of the new Liberal ministry, notice of which is set forth in the throne speech.
May I first commend the government for its decision to present legislation to the house to establish a municipal loan fund. This is good news for the mayors' federation of Canada, which sought in vain for such a fund from the previous government. They made representations on this matter in 1961 to the Senate committee on manpower and employment. Extensive justification in support of the federation's carefully drawn conclusions is set forth in report No. 10 of the Senate committee proceedings dated February 15, 1961.
Subsequent thereto the federation urged the then minister of finance, the former member for Eglinton, to recognize the urgent need for national government action to implement the proposed fund. No decision was made at that time. Following the June 18, 1962 election no action was taken on this matter so vitally essential to any comprehensive plan to increase the opportunities for national employment and at the same time overtake the backlog of much needed municipal services and urban renewal programs. It could provide a potential alternative to foreign sources of funds and thus help to improve the nation's external payments position.
The government of the right hon. gentleman who now leads the official opposition further delayed a decision on this urgently needed policy by referring the question to the royal commission on banking and finance. On October 29, 1962 the mayors' federation submitted to that commission another extensive brief fully outlining the many economic advantages to be derived from a federal government municipal loan fund.
The Leader of the Opposition had much to say about the throne speech. On page 43 of Hansard for May 20 he is reported as follows:
I intend to deal with this speech from the throne, because in every part of Canada there is national disappointment. It is full of platitudes spaced out among economic generalities which indicate that the planners and the bureaucrats know best.
I am certain, Mr. Speaker, that the mayors of Canada, who submitted their brief on the need for a municipal loan fund to the royal commission on banking and finance, are not

disappointed with the Liberal ministry's decision to ask the house to establish a municipal loan fund. I am equally certain that the brief submitted by the mayors' federation on this matter is neither platitudinous nor the product of bureaucrats.
At this point it may be well to contrast the previous government's vacillation on this vital and urgent matter with the performance of the new Liberal ministry. On April 22 the right hon. gentleman from Algoma East (Mr. Pearson), who so capably leads the Liberal party, became Prime Minister. He proceeded with the appointment of his cabinet ministers and then went to work. On May 16, the day the house was opened, the throne speech reflected the decisions which had been made in the first 24 days of the new ministry. The Leader of the Opposition referred to the expression "60 days of decision" as "shifty days". The record of performance of this house on the specific recommendations of the new Liberal ministry will determine to which hon. member and to which party the term "shifty" should apply in the context used by the Leader of the Opposition.
I reiterate that the throne speech reflects the decision of the new ministry to establish a municipal loan fund, a decision taken within 24 days contrasted to over two years of established shiftiness on this subject by the former government, which then ducked the issue by waiting for the report of the royal commission on banking and finance.
The throne speech also provides other conclusive evidence of decisive action on the part of the new Liberal ministry within the 24-day period from April 22 to May 16. During those 24 days of decision the government decided to introduce measures at the current session of this twenty sixth parliament to establish a new department of industry to foster industrial expansion throughout Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to add my congratulations to those of hon. members who have spoken ahead of me in this debate to yourself and to your deputy upon appointment to these high offices. I understand from those who have been in this house for years that the choices are excellent. I should like also to congratulate the Prime Minister and the members of the cabinet upon their appointments to posts of high responsibility. and I am confident this is the general situation throughout Canada. Therefore I reject the suggestion that our economy is not already rolling. What I do suggest is that we keep it rolling, by co-operation in this house of minorities.

Imitation is the sincerest form of flattery, and when it is done on this scale it borders on adulation. I was delighted to discover how much the government learned during its years in opposition. Therefore, on our part, and speaking particularly on my own behalf, I say that in the days to come we will no doubt be able to support many of the policies outlined in the speech from the throne because so many of them are directly derived from the policies of the previous government.
However, there were some omissions from that speech, one example of which was that there was no proposed action regarding a national medicare plan, in which I, as a member of the medical profession, am deeply interested. Many items were conspicuous by their absence, but I hope this may be corrected as the session proceeds. While I came to the house to be critical in a constructive way of the government's action and legislation which I may consider lacking, I also come in a spirit of co-operation, a spirit which the last parliament so sadly lacked. I stand to support strong legislation introduced by the government. Indeed it is our responsibility to do so, but in turn we expect the government to be responsive to constructive and indulgent criticism, and to ensure that the legislation proposed is respected in every detail. There should be no need to remind the government that every member of the house is a legislator, and that their views should be given proper and fair consideration.
I should like to deal now with four items about which I am particularly concerned, and which were dealt with inadequately or not at all in the speech from the throne. Brief mention was made about assistance for the completion of the trans-Canada highway. This, of course, is a continuation of the policy of previous governments, but there was no mention of any move to establish a national highway system or to bring about the formation of a national highways policy. This, Mr. Speaker, you will recall is something which the Conservative government had included in its program for Canada, and I would urge the present government not to hesitate to follow that lead, having done so in so many other ways.
The Address-Mr. Willoughby
It was a Conservative government which completed the first railroad across Canada and a Conservative government which ensured that this country would have a trans-Canada highway as a link from the Pacific to the Atlantic. I hope the new government will learn from such examples and begin working on the formulation of a national highways policy, recognizing the primary jurisdiction of the provinces over highway construction. It is going to become more and more necessary to establish some procedure of coordination among the various highway programs in order to bring about a proper system as soon as possible. As Canada grows, and as the provinces continue to build more and more highways, it is important that we should soon decide on co-ordination of the provincial highway programs, and that consideration be given to completion of a second trans-Canada highway.
Highways are not only the heart, arteries and lifeblood of modern transportation, but they are like a roll of beautiful ribbon; as they unravel they carry with them new populations, new industry, new employment and new prosperity. Never was this better demonstrated than since the opening of the Rogers pass route last year. As a specific proposal I would urge this government to include the Yellowhead highway pass in the scheme I have suggested for a national highway system. Its benefits would equal those already realized by the completion of the Rogers pass route. I am not suggesting, of course, that the federal government try to do this alone, but I do suggest that at the earliest possible time the federal government call together a conference of provincial highway ministers under the chairmanship of the federal Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) to discuss this very important question.
There was mention of the Columbia river treaty. I listened with great interest to the hon. member from Kootenay West (Mr. Her-ridge) when he spoke on this important subject on May 24. He would suggest that radical changes are necessary to make this agreement acceptable. Well, Mr. Speaker, I am not an engineer, but I am prepared to accept the reports and agreements devised by the best engineers of both Canada and the United States who, after 17 years of negotiations, arrived at the most acceptable solution to all concerned. In any such negotiations one side cannot have it all its own way, but the treaty as outlined today is the most acceptable to all parties. I feel it is vital that parliament ratify the treaty in its present form, and as soon as possible.
I note that the Prime Minister is to meet the premier of British Columbia to discuss this matter. I wish him luck at this meeting,

The Address-Mr. Willoughby and I fervently hope that it takes place. The premier has already demonstrated a distressing habit of forgetting appointments. At this meeting these should be no backing down before the connivances of Mr. Bennett, and connivances there will be. It is the first responsibility of the government to protect Canadian resources, and any suggestion of bowing to the pressure of Mr. Bennett would be an abrogation of that responsibility.
May I urge, therefore, that the federal government stand firm on the Columbia river treaty as it was signed, because it is vital to the future development of British Columbia. I understand from a radio news broadcast the other evening that the Minister of Forestry (Mr. Nicholson), whose opinion I respect, stated in Vancouver on Friday last that no radical change in the treaty is anticipated or necessary. At least these words are encouraging.
Mr. Speaker, I want to bring to the attention of the government the absence of any reference to a policy regarding feed grain assistance for British Columbia. This, you may recall, was included in the program devised by the former minister of agriculture. This is important to the ranchers and farmers of British Columbia. At the present time beef ranchers in our part of the country are compelled to ship their range cattle to the prairies for market processing, instead of bringing the grain from the prairies to the interior of British Columbia, because of the high cost of feed grain purchased through the wheat board. I therefore want to impress upon this house the need for the introduction of a proper policy in this regard in the immediate future.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I want to bring to the attention of the government the complete lack in the throne speech of any indication that the government recognizes the need for forward looking policies to deal with the problems of our Indian citizens. I hope that the Indian claims commission proposed by the Conservative government will be established even though there was no reference to it in the throne speech. Our Indian citizens need our help so they can share fully in Canada's growth and development.
I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that I do appreciate the opportunity provided for me to speak, and I hope the suggestions I have had to offer and will offer in the future will not be considered as frivolous or unjustified but that they may be of assistance to good government in our country. As I attempt to follow my predecessor's example, I feel it is my duty to speak out fearlessly in the interests of Kamloops riding and the interests of Canada. In return I anticipate just and courteous consideration from all departments of this great national assembly.

I may perhaps be permitted to note that in the opposite gallery is sitting another former minister of the crown, a distinguished and gallant gentleman, Hon. Milton Gregg, former minister of labour.
Mr. Speaker, I now wish to make a report on the ministerial meeting of NATO which was held in Ottawa last week. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) and I had the responsibility of representing the government of Canada at that meeting. Because of the importance of the subject matter, and in accordance with the convention which attends the delivery of a statement of this importance by a minister of the crown, I propose to follow closely what I have prepared for this particular occasion.
May I say at the outset that it was an excellent idea, in my judgment, to have Canada play host to this meeting. Thanks to the superb physical arrangements made through the co-operative efforts of various departments of government under the able chairmanship of General Fin Clark, chairman of the national capital commission, a most favourable impression, I am sure, has been made upon our distinguished visitors.
I cannot too highly commend those who were associated with this preparatory work over ' a period of some four months.

In addition, of course, the Minister of National Defence and I were afforded an opportunity to meet our opposite numbers both during and before the ministerial meeting itself. I had valuable talks in my office in the four days preceding the meeting with secretary of state Rusk, foreign minister Lord Home, and with the foreign ministers of France, M. Couve de Murville, and of Germany, Mr. Schroeder; that is, with the leading members and representatives at this meeting of those countries with which we have the most intimate relations. Of course I should add, so that I would not in any way discriminate, that I was privileged to have important and useful talks with the foreign ministers of Holland, Belgium, Portugal, Turkey, Greece and Denmark. We were able to review not only matters which would be brought before the meeting, but also questions of bilateral concern. In ordinary circumstances it might have taken many months to establish direct personal contact with these foreign ministers or, in the case of the Minister of National Defence, with ministers of national defence from the 14 countries which attended the ministerial meeting along with Canada. All this, 1 must say, is due to the forethought of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) in having invited the conference to Ottawa last December.
(Translation):
During the private talks I had with our distinguished visitors, I felt that they were deeply conscious of the fact that the success of the alliance would in the end depend on our being able to combine the efforts of western Europe, and North America.
In years gone by, such a partnership could exist only through mutual understanding between Great Britain and the U.S.A. Canada has played a useful role in that field at various times. The happy relations between London and Washington are the results of such steps.
Now that Europe has recovered from war devastation, the Atlantic community must be given a broader basis.
As a North American country which has received a precious inheritance and two cultures from its motherlands, Canada can once more be useful in exerting a discreet influence to promote even greater understanding among the members of the Atlantic alliance.
(Text):
Mr. Speaker, this meeting was timely in another sense. It gave the government an opportunity to remove the doubts which continued to linger in the minds of our allies concerning the position of Canada with regard to the commitments undertaken on be-
The Address-Hon. P. Martin half of our armed forces by the former government. To that end the Minister of National Defence took the opportunity on the first day of the conference to set the record straight by confirming to the council in ministerial session the information which had already been given to parliament two days before by the Prime Minister, namely that negotiations had been resumed with the United States relating to defensive nuclear weapons systems which had been the subject of previous discussions with the United States.
I want to make perfectly clear that Canada has undertaken no new commitments at the meeting just concluded. It is, however, the policy of this government to take the steps needed to make it possible for the Canadian forces to discharge the role accepted for them by the previous government. This was as long ago as 1959. That role would not disappear if Canada failed to carry it out; all that would happen would be that some other member or members of the alliance would have to shoulder the obligation in our place.
The kind of forces Canada agreed to contribute were to meet part of an established NATO military requirement, and I am sure that no hon. member of this house would wish Canada to be placed in the position where it would be foisting upon others a task voluntarily assumed by Canada through the former government as part of the collective defence effort of the alliance. I stress the word "voluntarily" because the military contributions to meet agreed force requirements were assumed as a result of bilateral discussions between the NATO military authorities and individual member states, and not all of them saw fit to undertake a nuclear role. I will have more to say a little later in connection with this aspect of the NATO meeting.
Now, sir, the spring ministerial meeting of the NATO council is normally attended by foreign ministers to review international developments and appraise the state of the alliance. Defence ministers also participated at this time because there were on the agenda items affecting the organization of the deterrent forces at the disposal of the alliance.
