The decisions on defence matters taken at the meeting have attracted a great deal of public notice, virtually to the exclusion of all else. I do not wish to underrate the significance of those decisions, for they represented a further step in the integration of elements of the deterrent forces which should go some distance toward improving their co-ordination and control. But I would also draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that the emphasis in the communique was on peace. The communique opened and closed on that note. This is as it should be, for ours is a defensive alliance, the military activities of which are maintained solely in the interests of the integrity of the member states and therefore of the peace of the world. The whole underlying concept of NATO is the prevention of war, and there is full realization within the alliance that peace cannot be ensured by military power alone. So the council has reasserted its desire to seek equitable solutions by negotiation, and it is hoped that the communist world will come to see that they too have no less an interest in such settlements.
Some of the areas of continuing concern- Berlin, Cuba and Laos-are named in the communique and were indeed thoroughly discussed in the private sessions of the council. I reported to the council on the unsatisfactory situation in Laos from the viewpoint of one of the members of the three-nation international supervisory commission. I expressed our determination to continue to press for greater freedom of action and movement for the commission, and I am happy to know that the three members of the commission have joined together in their most recent report.
Too often in the past the council has met in the shadow of crisis. Last December it met in the immediate aftermath of Cuba. The preceding year it was the wall in Berlin. This year we were faced with no immediate threat of armed aggression affecting the treaty area directly, and this fact was noted in our review of the international situation. On the other hand the absence of war or the threat of war is a long way from the kind of peace we seek, and we were also forced to recognize that long standing issues such as were named in the communique remain unresolved and are a continuing source of grave concern. The causes of the present lull well may lie within the Sino-Soviet bloc itself, although no one can predict how long this state of immobility in east-west relations may continue.

There was complete agreement upon the importance of maintaining continuous contact with the Soviet union in an effort to resolve issues which might lead to war and ensure, at the very least, that neither side should misunderstand the intentions of the other.
In this connection the decision in principle which has been reached at Geneva between the United States and the Soviet union to establish direct communication between Washington and Moscow was welcomed by the Canadian delegation as one which should help to reduce the risk of war by miscalculation.
That agreement was one of the useful by-products of the 18-nation disarmament conference now meeting in Geneva. As I had occasion to say in one of my interventions before the council, the outlook at the Geneva disarmament conference and the test ban talks is so far from encouraging that it would be unrealistic to slacken our defence efforts. But I noted at the same time that the implications in both military and financial terms of an unrestricted arms race are such that we simply could not relax our efforts to negotiate a balanced reduction of armaments and armed forces provided we can secure the proper safeguards. To abandon this search would be a counsel of despair, although I have no illusions about either the ease or the speed with which results may be achieved.
There was unanimous support for the continuation of efforts at Geneva to bring about general and complete disarmament by stages under effective international control and international safeguards. Even though real progress in the scaling down of arms may be some distance away-and I believe this is the case-there are related areas such as the communications link which can substantially reduce the risk of war by accident or miscalculation and thereby contribute to the maintenance of peace and security. Similarly, on the subject of the nuclear test ban, I welcomed on behalf of the Canadian delegation and the government of Canada the recent Anglo-American approach in Moscow in an attempt to break the current deadlock. I made clear the Canadian view that there must be unremitting effort to bridge the narrow gap between east and west on this issue. Verification is, as it has so often been, the root of the trouble.
In our appraisal at the council meeting of the state of the alliance a good deal of attention was paid to the improvement and intensification of timely consultation on political developments. This is a subject on which members of this government have had a good deal of experience, in that the Prime Minister was intimately associated in 1955

with the specially appointed group which originally set up the procedures and basic rules which have been followed in the alliance ever since. Since taking over my responsibilities I have found that impressive strides have been made in this field in the intervening years, but in that same period there has been a corresponding growth in the scope and complexity of the problems facing the members of the alliance which demands an even more intensive effort in this direction. I took the occasion, in reviewing this question as seen from the Canadian viewpoint, to make clear that any shortcomings there may have been on the Canadian side would be removed.
I should like to make clear to the house, as I did to our NATO colleagues, that the Canadian government looks upon its contribution to NATO, and indeed regards the military role of the alliance itself, as part of a broad international network of peace keeping activities. As the Prime Minister indicated in his remarks at the opening ceremony, the interdependence of all nations is a distinctive characteristic of our era. It has come to be recognized that a local war, whether in Indo-China or Africa, if not contained, can have as grave consequences as any outbreak of hostilities in the more familiar trouble spots of direct concern to NATO. Moreover, participation in many of these peace keeping responsibilities outside the NATO area is, by tacit consent, denied to the major powers since one of the primary objects is to prevent fighting without inviting the even greater danger of a great power confrontation. For this reason it has been and continues to be Canadian policy to assume international peace keeping obligations both inside the United Nations, as in Gaza or the Congo, and outside, as in the Indo-China commissions. Through these activities we have a constant reminder that the NATO alliance has to be seen in a broad world perspective.
To place NATO in global context in this way, is not, however, in any way to deny that the central challenge to today's world is between the closed totalitarian regimes of the communist bloc and the free societies of the west, and that NATO is the instrument on which we all rely to meet that challenge. One of the principal subjects with which we were concerned at this meeting was the possible nature of that challenge, and to ensure that NATO forces should be so equipped as to be able to offer a range of responses appropriate to any aggression affecting the treaty area. In this connection two decisions of importance to Canada and to the alliance were taken, both of which were noted in the communique.
The first was concerned with the ability of the alliance to deal with the obvious threat
The Address-Hon. P. Martin posed by the Soviet union's mounting arsenal of nuclear weapons. Paragraph 8 of the communique described decisions taken by the council to regroup and organize certain elements of the nuclear deterrent forces under the command of the supreme allied commander Europe. These forces will henceforth include the whole of the United Kingdom V-bomber force and three United States Polaris submarines. This formidable new strength to be at the disposal of SACEUR will be added to certain tactical nuclear forces already in being or programmed and already assigned to him. This decision was of direct relevance to Canadian forces in Europe for, by indicating our willingness to arm the Canadian air division with the weapons which will enable it to discharge the strike role to which it was committed by the previous government, the way has been opened to permit Canada to play its part in the new arrangements.
Let me make it perfectly clear this decision in no way makes Canada a member of the nuclear club in the sense of owning or manufacturing nuclear warheads. Indeed, the decisions taken at this meeting affecting the organization of the alliance's existing nuclear forces are entirely consistent with resolutions unanimously adopted by the United Nations to avoid the further spread of nuclear weapons under independent national control. Custody of the nuclear armament of all the forces involved, with the exception of the United Kingdom bombers, will remain as before with the United States. I also want to make it clear that there is no new assignment involved for Canadian forces, as they were already assigned by the previous government to SACEUR's command. These arrangements were welcomed by the Canadian delegation as steps which, through the greater sharing of knowledge and responsibility for nuclear defence, will help to knit the alliance together and, in the words of the communique, "improve co-ordination and control of its nuclear deterrent forces".

The steps I mentioned earlier should be seen as part of the democratization of the alliance with respect to the exercise of its heavy responsibilities in the nuclear field.
The second decision of importance is recorded in paragraph 9 of the communique, where the need to achieve a satisfactory balance between nuclear and conventional forces was recognized. To this end the permanent council has been instructed to undertake, with the advice of the NATO military authorities, a comprehensive review of the interrelated questions of strategy, force requirements and the resources available to meet them. I have already mentioned that NATO must be able to offer a range of responses to any challenge, and this means that if that challenge is conventional then the conventional means must be available to meet it without premature recourse to nuclear weapons. At the same time the nuclear strength must be there to deter any possibility of a direct challenge with nuclear weapons.
The cost of maintaining the correct balance must be shared equitably amongst the members of the alliance and must be geared to the capabilities of each, having regard to its resources and its other military obligations.

This meeting of the council had before it certain matters for decision designed to reinforce the enduring character of the partnership between western Europe and North America. It took those decisions unanimously and in a spirit of harmony. It is wrong to say NATO is in a state of disarray. The assembled ministers were responding in a tangible way to the keynote address of one who has from the beginning lent inspiration to the alliance. I refer to the Prime Minister of Canada. The wise counsel he gave in opening the meeting, his assessment of NATO's achievements, his warning of the perils that lie ahead and his plea for unity created the climate for a meeting that will be recorded, I believe, in the history of the alliance as another milestone in Atlantic partnership.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to take part in this debate I should like, first of all, to congratulate you and the Deputy Speaker as well as the chairman of committees on your appointment to your high posts. I am sure that you will all fill these posts with sincerity and fairness to all members of this house. I should like also to congratulate the mover (Miss Jewett) and seconder (Mr. Cho-quette) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
I did not intend to get into an argument with the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin). However, after listening to him split hairs for the last 30 minutes regarding nuclear weapons, and refusing to answer the questions of the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), I am reminded of a quotation I should like to put on the record. There are a great many quotations I could put on the record, but none is better than the one I have in my hand to illustrate to the people of Canada how the Liberals have changed their mind about nuclear weapons. This is a quotation attributed to the Nobel peace prize recipient, the Right Hon. L. B. Pearson, and it appeared in the United Church Observer for October, 1961. It reads as follows:
We should not join the nuclear club by acceptance of nuclear weapons under national or so-called joint control. This would add little security to Canada or to the alliance and would be an abandonment of the stand we have taken at the United Nations and elsewhere, that the number of states possessing nuclear weapons should be limited rather than extended. Canada, if she became a nuclear power, would have far less influence and authority at the United Nations than she has had in the past-
This was the stand taken in 1961. Now, the big-wigs of the party have changed their minds. They keep changing their minds so often that we do not know where we are, and I do not believe they do either.
Now, Mr. Speaker, the election resulted in a new government taking office. I do not feel there was any need for that election because we had a good government in power. If you go back and look at the record you will find, as the Ottawa Journal did, that national production in 1962 had climbed 8 per cent to a peak of $40,400 million, the greatest increase in any western country during this time. After years of trade deficits, we achieved a favourable trade balance. Foreign exchange reserves in U.S. currency reached a total of $2,700 million, the greatest reached in years.

The Address-Mr. Smallwood Trade had reached an all-time high; manufacturing had jumped by 8 per cent, construction by 8.2 per cent and capital investment by 4.8 per cent. This editorial concludes by saying:
We must all hope that Mr. Pearson does well; to wish him well is but to wish well for Canada. But for truth's sake, if for nothing else, let Mr. Pearson and his friends stop trying to give the impression that they took over a broken down Canadian economy.
They did nothing of the kind. They wanted to obtain power. X could refer you to an editorial that appeared in the Toronto Globe and Mail which reads:
The Liberals went into opposition in 1957 after 22 years in power. They had in their ranks a number of former cabinet ministers who had the opportunity to offer informed and instructive criticism; who had the opportunity over the past four years to devise detailed alternative policies to those proclaimed by the government.
The Liberal leaders chose not to use their opportunities in a serious or responsible manner. Instead, they chose to offer negative and destructive criticism, to cry gloom and doom for the country, and to spend the rest of their time fashioning new planks to fasten on the shaky structure of the Liberal welfare state.
The Liberals came here after the 1962 election with one objective in mind and that was to force an election as soon as they could. They could not do this themselves, but needed the support of the other two groups we have in the corner. During the campaign, we heard the Social Credit members talking about Canada being ruled by the Liberals and the Conservatives. The other day in this chamber I heard one of the New Democratic members stand up and chant the same old cry that for 90 years Canada had been ruled by the Liberals and the Conservatives.

Let us look at British Columbia. Mr. Speaker, under the Social Credit government in B.C. provincial debt rose from $218 million in 1952 to $1,260,000,000 today. That is what Social Credit is doing in British Columbia.

Why, you Social Crediters can make figures read any way you like. During the election campaign the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) visited my home town. About 400 or 500 people attended his meeting, and he went back to Red Deer

and told his constituents that he had the constituency of Battle River-Camrose won. One of my friends attended that meeting, and I asked him what the Social Credit leader had to say. He replied "I listened for 40 minutes; when I left I was still waiting for him to say something." Only last week the hon. member for Red Deer treated the house to one of his old, warmed over speeches.
During the election campaign the hon. member for Red Deer went out to Vancouver and said something about Premier Manning being included in the federal cabinet if Social Credit won the election, but on March 26, 1963, there was this report in the Edmonton Journal:
Thompson claim said unfounded-Premier E. C. Manning termed a report by national Social Credit Leader Robert Thompson as "wholly unwarranted and without foundation."
Mr. Thompson said Sunday in Vancouver at a press conference that Premier Manning would likely be in the cabinet if his party won the April 8 federal election.
Mr. Manning told the Journal Monday: "I am certain Mr. Thompson had no intention of conveying the impression taken from his comments at Vancouver, as we have had no discussion on this matter."
Such was the irresponsibility of these people going around and making remarks like that, but this time the people of Canada showed that we have no place for splinter group parties in Canadian politics. I say to those on the left, move over with the Liberals, and to those on the right, move in with the Conservatives, and let us get ahead with the business of government.

speechtext: Look at your own party and the splinters in it.

speechtext:
Don't scratch your head, you may get some slivers. Mr. Speaker, the throne speech was nothing more than a warmed over edition of the policies introduced by the Conservative government. We heard an awful lot about the devaluation of the dollar, and I remember the hue and cry in 1962 on the part of Liberal front benchers when we devalued the dollar. They said it was a terrible thing; but on looking back I find that on September 16, 1939 and July 5, 1946 the Canadian dollar was devalued to 90.5 cents under the Liberal government. It was the same from 1949 to 1950.
Devaluation of the Canadian dollar helped the economy of our country, but it is interesting note in the Canadian Liberal Challenge, the newspaper put out by the Liberal party headquarters in December 1962, there was a question from the New York Times magazine which reads as follows:
The ultimate humiliation came this summer when the government was forced to devalue the Canadian dollar. It was pegged at 921 United States cents.
The Address-Mr. Smallwood
However I notice the Minister of Finance realizes now that it was a good move, and I am glad he is content to leave the dollar pegged where it is. That quotation from the New York Times magazine also said this:
With winter, their hardest season, coming close, Canadians now wait to see how deep the economic crisis will cut and how severe austerity will be. They are resigned to higher prices as a result of the import surtax.
What happened, Mr. Speaker? The price of living in Canada rose slightly over 1.6 per cent since last fall, the smallest increase in the western world. They talk about the economic conditions of the country, but on February 13 last the Ottawa Journal had this to say:
Mr. Pearson and his much-vaunted economic wizard, Mr. Walter Gordon used to talk about the decline of our gross national product. They are not talking that way now. The gross national product is on its way up now; for 1962 it is estimated at 8.2 per cent over 1961.
Elsewhere in the article it says:
Well, only a few days ago President Kennedy produced facts to show that in the matter of economic stability Canada's 1962 record was better than "any other western industrial nation"-common market countries included.
When these people talked about doom and gloom they had no desire but to get back into power, regardless of the truth and regardless of what they put before the Canadian people.
They talked about unemployment. Well, Mr. Speaker, there was unemployment under the previous Liberal government. In fact I can quote from the "Western Canadian Lumber Worker" of November 1951 in which a Social Credit supporter said "5 per cent unemployment good for Canada".
An unemployed level of 5 per cent of the working force would be a good thing for the Canadian economy, says E. W. Hinman, Alberta's provincial treasurer.
That is just one more example of irresponsibility on the part of those people. We have helped the unemployment situation and I only hope the Liberal government will bring in amendments to the Unemployment Insurance Act, because it is grossly unfair that people who do not wish to work can get unemployment insurance. However, the government has to have the support of the cities and municipalities in order to help clear up unemployment, and when I speak of cities and municipalities no better example comes to my mind than the city of Ottawa, where they hire women on the traffic squad. They putt up and down the streets on their scooters checking the meters and they stand out on the streets directing traffic. This is certainly no job for a woman. It does not add any dignity to the city of Ottawa and, above all, it is taking work from men; there are many

The Address-Mr. Smallwood family men who could do this work and I am sure these women could find work more suitable to them than out directing traffic.
I am sorry the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) has left the chamber because I wish to say I am a little concerned about the displacement of many people in government service. I am speaking of Liberal patronage, because that party has a great system for passing out patronage. We can remember how the only commissioner from western Canada on the veterans pension board was displaced not very long ago, but shortly after we came into power the inspector on the ships in Montreal was known to be in possession of contraband spirits and tobacco and I can remember all the fight we had from across the floor then.
Last year the former member for Assini-boia got up in this house and made a big speech about the P.F.A. political machine which the Conservative minister of agriculture was supposed to have. The hon. member must not have known very much about political machines. He should have seen the one the Liberals had before we got into power. I happen to know a man who attended a P.F.A. school in a town in Alberta. He said there were about 90 men there and the man in charge told them "You people are all good Liberals or you would not be here today." He told them to go out and take up the P.F.A. claims, but not to take more than eight, and to preach Liberal policies to the farmers when they were doing it. I hope the present government will not return to such low standards as that. They should be able to spread Liberal propaganda across western Canada without that and without using treasury money. In my constituency I have Liberals, Social Crediters and-no, I do not think I have any Social Crediters.

speechtext: Don't discriminate.

speechtext:
I am not discriminating; I want ability. I have Liberals and Conservatives taking up P.F.A., and if the Liberals try to fire all those people they will be firing all the people who used to support them.
My time is limited, Mr. Speaker, and I want to come now to agriculture. The minister is unfortunately not here today. I have with me a pamphlet entitled "Prosperity on the farm" and another entitled "Time for action", both published by the national Liberal federation. These are handy little pamphlets to carry around. The first one says, with regard to wheat, oats and barley, that a Liberal government will immediately bring in a price of $2 a bushel for No. 1 northern. They went across the country saying this and the Prime Minister promised the farmer $2 a bushel for his wheat. Now the 60 days of action have almost gone and I do not see any move


toward keeping the promise they made. They promised a two price system under the unit quota. Before they go into that I hope they will give it a little study, because if they start paying out money under the unit quota they will see 25 per cent of the farmers getting 75 per cent of the money, and they will be neglecting the little farmer whose friend they are supposed to be. Therefore I hope they give these matters a little consideration before they go too far with some of their new ideas. This pamphlet also says that a new Liberal government would establish a higher initial price for oats and barley, which would be announced well before seeding. Well, they have not many members here from western Canada but I will tell them that a lot of oats and barley are going into the ground today. When is this going to happen? Probably five years from now. They will not be in power then.
We also see that they are going to appoint an associate minister of agriculture. I agree that they should appoint an associate minister of agriculture, but this idea of appointing a minister of agriculture for western Canada and one for eastern Canada is nothing more than trying to split the country down the middle. It just will not work. It is fine to have one minister of agriculture for Canada and an associate minister to work with him, but if they are going to try and split Canada down the' middle by having a minister of agriculture in the west and one in the east, it is just not going to work.
I know the west was neglected for 22 years by the Liberals. Sometimes I blame them and sometimes I do not, because I look back and see that we sent C.C.F'ers and Social Crediters from western Canada for 22 years, and I wonder whether I should blame them. Today western Canada has sent some farmers to put through a good farm policy. That is what the people of this country want. We have to get back to a stable government. We went out and sold our wheat when the Liberals were in power. The minister of trade and commerce in the Liberal government had the attitude, "We have the wheat. If you want it, come and get it". That was the attitude of the Liberals, but our attitude was to get out and sell the wheat. We passed the Export Credits Insurance Act which put money into the hands of the department and enabled them to sell our wheat. We got out and sold wheat to China. We were condemned by some hon. members who said it was immoral to sell wheat to China. It is not immoral to sell food to any country that is starving.
I say to the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp), send your delegations out and sell our wheat. If you keep prosperity

in western agriculture, this will bring prosperity to the manufacturing communities in the east, because the western farmer will go out and buy expensive machinery, every piece of machinery that he requires for his farm in western Canada. This will in turn bring more employment to eastern Canada. Therefore I hope that in the next few weeks we will see some good agricultural legislation come before this house. If it is good for the welfare of the farmers of Canada, I will be one of the first to support it.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is traditional, of course, that I should join the other hon. members who have spoken in this debate on the speech from the throne in offering you my congratulations. I do so with the knowledge of the help, guidance and assistance which you so kindly accorded to me when I came into the house for the first time last June. I would like, also, to take this opportunity of congratulating the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I was happy to see them continue in the same fine tradition that characterized the speech of the mover last session, the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Chaplin).
If I may be excused, Mr. Speaker, I would like to cross the line of party politics for the moment and voice my regret at the absence from this hallowed chamber of many of the fine speakers who contributed so ably to the debates last year. I think I perhaps listened to more speeches than the average member. I miss the gentle responses of the former secretary of state for external affairs, and I miss more than anything, I think, the clear logic and to-the-point speeches of the then hon. member for York South. If I in no way share the political philosophy of that hon. member who is no longer in the house, I at least admired his contribution to the House of Commons in the short time he was here.
Mr. Speaker, may I also draw the attention of all hon. members of this house to the remarks made the other evening by the hon. member from Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) pertaining to the conservation of the rights and privileges which we have acquired in this House of Commons through so many years of trial and tribulation. I hope that in our haste for parliamentary reform we do not substitute speed for efficiency.
I think there is one thing this parliament can do without. That is a continuation of the vicious anti-American campaign that characterized Tory efforts in the last election. I think many of the speeches from that side of the chamber so far have indicated that they intend to carry that anti-American campaign into the house. I think this type of action is
The Address-Mr. Mackasey but a reflection upon the integrity of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), and the constant references to his trip to Hyannis Port and to the United States press, radio and television is also an insult to the people of Canada, who showed clearly in the last election that they want no part of any anti-Americanism in this house.
Mr. Speaker, there has also been more than a little reference to the 60 days of decision. I think this is no doubt the role of the opposition. But I think, the very fact that we are here so soon after the election should be taken as some indication of good faith on the part of the Prime Minister. Certainly if the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) succeeds in bringing down a budget within 60 days, as he has already promised, he will have done more than the previous minister of finance was able to do in two years.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may be permitted for just a moment, before discussing the speech from the throne, to say a few words on behalf of the community which I represent. Like so many others represented here in the house, my community could, I suppose, be labelled bilingual. We have no agricultural content and no industrial complex, but we rank in population with a third of the province of Quebec. We have acquired the reputation, Mr. Speaker, of being perhaps the most community-minded city in Canada. Certainly the No. 4 Legion branch has carried on in that tradition, and as I mentioned in the address in reply to the speech from the throne last year we are very proud of the fact that we in the city of Verdun can boast that we had the highest rate of voluntary enlistment in the Canadian army of any city of comparable size during the last war. Just a few weeks ago we were one of the few cities across Canada to mark the commemoration of the battles of Ypres in appropriate style.
I may say that I, like other hon. members who have already spoken, would like to see medicare introduced, and introduced soon. I should like to see the Liberals maintain their promise of university grants to leading students. I am aware of the fact, however, that all cannot be accomplished at the first session, but I am sure that we will be constantly reminded of this vital social legislation which we need so badly.
In my own community, Mr. Speaker, there is one piece of legislation sadly needed, and that is some federal program to provide housing for our senior citizens. I like to use the term "senior citizens" when talking of our aged, for they are precisely that. They are the people who have made their contribution to this country of ours. They are not looking for handouts but simply for some

The Address-Mr. Mackasey way to exist, at the same time retaining their dignity and pride. I think that in my community at least private industry has failed in regard to providing housing for our senior citizens.
Mr. Speaker, there is another item in the speech from the throne which is of concern to me. I am referring, of course, to the establishment of a commission on bicul-turalism and bilingualism. The hon. member for iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Sauve), whom I admire and respect greatly, made a very fine and moving speech on this subject last week. I would urge all hon. members who were not present to read Hansard and his interpretation of the problems that are confronting the province of Quebec. He made no attempt to assess the blame for this unhappy situation; rather he simply emphasized the facts as they existed. He has suggested, and rightly so I think, that the economic plight of the average citizen of Quebec as compared with that of, for example, Ontario was one of the underlying factors in the unrest in Quebec today. I do not attempt to place the blame for the unrest in Quebec on the shoulders of any particular party represented in this house; I think we are all to blame.
Mr. Speaker, I was therefore quite happy when the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) lived up to his promise made last fall of establishing such a royal commission. I think it was the first and the most logical step suggested in this house to recognize the problems of French Canada. I was hoping, Mr. Speaker, that such a commission might bring to the surface some of the subtle differences which have caused friction in that province; and I speak with some little concern and knowledge of the matter for I am one of the many hundreds of thousands of English speaking Canadians who dwell in the province of Quebec. I was born, as a matter of fact, in the cradle of this country, the city of Quebec, and at an early age I moved to a village known as Sillery, which produced the famous Chubby Power, who graced this House of Commons for many years.
Mr. Speaker, there are many differences which are separating Quebec from the rest of the country, and certainly with the time at my disposal I could name but few of them. But I should like hon. members to remember that the rights which the French Canadians are asking for themselves across the country are the rights that I, as a representative of the English minority, have always enjoyed in the province of Quebec. I can remember, Mr. Speaker, going to school for the first time 35 years ago. I was entitled to attend an

English speaking school with English speaking teachers, and with a curriculum acceptable to the religious beliefs of my parents. This privilege has always been recognized in the province of Quebec. Certainly French Canadians, in asking for this privilege in other parts of Canada, are simply asking for things which they have always extended to the minority in our province. The use of English in the provincial buildings, in civic administration, even in road signs, periodicals and annual reports, has always been encouraged and fully recognized. The maintenance of the rights and privileges of the minority in our province, even in the dark days of Mr. Duplessis, has always been protected. Personally, as one who is considered reasonably bilingual, I cannot visualize the day when every Canadian will be fully bilingual, but I do think the day has come when every Canadian should have more than a passing interest in French or English; and I might add, Mr. Speaker, that my remarks apply equally to my French Canadian friends.
Rather than wait for the full implementation of the royal commission report, I think steps can be taken immediately to further the cause of bilingualism, at least in our senior civil service departments. I do not subscribe to the theory that all must be rectified by 1967. Certainly there is no magic date when all these differences of opinion must disappear. But I do think that confederation should at least mark the date of stocktaking, when we can look back with pride to some improvement in the question of bilingualism and biculturalism. I think, Mr. Speaker, that every Canadian is duty bound to acquaint himself a little more with French Canada. Prominent Canadians found to their delight many years ago that a deep knowledge of French Canada, its culture, its language and its traditions is an exciting and fulfilling experience. The province of Quebec is our birthplace, and it was from here that the hardy settlers first braved the tough winters and journeyed on to make Canada, and indeed the United States, known to our European friends.
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I may be permitted for just a moment to outline some of the facts which have led to the rejuvenation of the province of Quebec. The fact that in 1960 our province was finally freed from the yoke of a very corrupt administration is, I think, well known to all of us, and certainly if the province of Quebec has not expanded as well as it should have economically, the blame must not be laid entirely at the feet of English Canadians. French Canadians must take a second look at the yoke of tyranny which men like Duplessis placed around their own necks. Today our province is on the

move. The institution of a hospital insurance plan, for example, brought it into line with the rest of the country. Our universities are flourishing, thanks to statutory grants. High school education is now free up to and including grade 11, and the province is embarking upon a vast building program for secondary and technical schools. Crown prosecutors are being named on a permanent basis.
Antiquated electoral laws have been brought up to date and Quebecers for the first time in history are putting their savings to use for the benefit of the province through their general finance corporation. Meanwhile, the council for economic orientation is endeavouring to spread industry beyond the confines of the upper St. Lawrence valley.
In short, I feel the province of Quebec is rapidly closing the economic gap which separates it from the rest of the country. Its culture is flourishing. Its literature and art are finding a ready audience not only in the United States but in English speaking Canada. Its French television programming is vigorous and alive; French technicians have been responsible for the finest of the documentary films made by the national film board.
I remain one of the optimists as far as the future of confederation is concerned. However, I believe confederation must be reviewed and its contents more clearly defined. It is important for us to remember that the terms of confederation will mean very little if there is not a desire to make them work, motivated by mutual respect and understanding. The desire for equality of opportunity, equality of language, must be earnestly desired by all Canadians and for all Canadians. Certainly I think we must realize that the spirit of confederation, as it was envisaged, has never been fully realized. The time has come for us to realize that what is good and proper for Quebec is good and proper for Canada. By the same token, French Canadians and the people of Quebec should realize that what is good for Canada is good for Quebec. It is not by isolation that Quebec will fulfil its destiny. It is not by retiring from confederation that Quebecers will realize the fulfilment of their economic dreams. The eventual and logical development of Quebec to the full richness of which Quebec is capable must come from within confederation. The time is now.
Canada is ready and willing to view the French Canadian position in its right perspective. It is not by loose talk of ten federations, of separatism or of reducing the role of the federal government to nothing that Quebec will flourish. It will flourish when Canadians right across this great dominion realize that the ultimate greatness of this country depends on a vigorous and lusty Quebec, and that our greatest protection against further inroads
The Address-Mr. Churchill into our culture by friendly allies is the extension of French Canadian culture across the country. I believe this fact has now been recognized across the nation. Responsible Canadians everywhere feel French Canada has been ignored to some extent. I believe Quebec has served notice in the last two years that it is fully capable of managing its own affairs. If the province is to achieve the greatness of which it is capable, her leaders must now be prepared to permit the rest of Canada to help rectify the situation.
In closing, may I say that if certain leaders in the field of politics and in the world of letters adopt the attitude that nothing can be done, that Quebec has no role to play in confederation, then the long struggle for equality will have been in vain. If, on the other hand, the commission on biculturalism is given an opportunity to function, if its report is analysed with an open mind, if the differences separating French Canada and English Canada are acted upon, then I feel Canada will eventually reach the greatness predicted for it by Sir Wilfrid Laurier.

Mr. Speaker, I wish I had time to deal extensively with the speech made this afternoon by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), but I have certain other topics to deal with, so I cannot do more than comment briefly on the remarks he made.
The minister, who had an opportunity to give us a full statement with regard to the NATO conference, satisfied himself with a rough and ready summary of what happened at those meetings. He forgot to mention that most of it had been decided in advance and that the communique had been prepared and agreed upon by most of the leading nations in NATO long before the business was concluded. The hon. gentleman did point out, though, that he had met in advance with various foreign ministers, starting off with Secretary Rusk, thus reversing the order followed a couple of weeks ago when the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) started off with the prime minister of the United Kingdom. Here, perhaps, we have the proposed pattern. The hon. gentleman began by meeting the secretary of state and followed by meeting Lord Home of the United Kingdom.
The minister of external affairs indicated to us that the debate on nuclear arms is far from finished. He opened up new vistas for us to examine. He indicated, as did the Prime Minister earlier, that the question of defence policy would be taken up when the committee is appointed to discuss that matter. The Prime Minister said it would be a committee to consider defence policy and the Secretary

The Address-Mr. Churchill of State for External Affairs said almost the same thing this afternoon. Consequently we shall have, to use his words, a review of national defence policy as soon as we get around to setting up the committee. It is essential we should do this because there is certainly great misunderstanding in regard to this subject, above all, in the mind of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. He had the effrontery to say that in the discussions prior to the meeting he took it upon himself to remove what he called doubts in the minds of our allies with regard to Canada's role in NATO. Mr. Speaker, there has never been any doubt in the minds of those in any country as to Canada's role in any crisis. There is no country in the world which has exceeded Canada's efforts in time of international crisis. Except for some of our own Canadian politicians, no person has ever expressed doubt about this country meeting its obligations in time of international crisis. Yet we find the minister of external affairs continuing this practice of downgrading Canada and leaving an impression in the minds of his listeners that in the past there have been doubts created in the minds of our allies-he means, of course, by the previous government. None of this happened during the days of the Eisenhower administration, and I am surprised that the minister of external affairs should use an expression like that in this house.
The hon. gentleman also indicated that Canada was now about to take steps to discharge the role to be played by our forces. There has never been any dispute or misunderstanding on the part of anyone suggesting that Canada would not discharge its role effectively. The hon. gentleman went on to say that the NATO meeting had direct relevance-those were his words because I took them down-to Canadian forces in Europe. Yet a few months ago gentlemen opposite were saying throughout this country that the NATO council to be assembled in Ottawa would have nothing whatever to do with Canada's role in defence. They told us earlier that only the foreign ministers would come. We discovered-and the Canadian people now realize-that the defence ministers came along as well, because the major item to be discussed at this meeting was the subject of defence. So the hon. gentleman had to admit that the NATO meeting last week had direct relevance to the employment of Canadian forces in Europe, as we said from the beginning. Then he went on to say -and it has been announced in the press- that the government had committed our forces to SACEUR and that they would now be a part of its deterrent force. I point out that

this new force which has been put together is a deterrent force comprised of the bomber fleet of the United Kingdom, three Polaris submarines and the tactical nuclear force available in Europe of which Canada's force comprises part. The government has taken action of this kind without reference to parliament and has committed our force in Europe to undertaking a deterrent role. It is not just a defensive force. The range of the planes is not very great but it is enough to enable them to reach into the iron curtain countries. The size of the bomb carried is such that it is not just a defensive bomb to be used in support of an army on the battlefield. It is a megaton bomb and there will be 144 planes each armed with a megaton bomb, which we are told is equivalent to the explosive power of a million tons of explosive. Canada itself will have enough explosive power virtually to destroy civilization.
So this government, without having a national review of Canada's defence policy, without referring the matter to parliament, has committed Canada now to a position in the deterrent force under NATO. I would have thought that this matter should be carefully considered by parliament and carefully considered by the people of Canada before precipitate action such as was taken. Here was the chance-the NATO meeting, proposals put forward there and then a full discussion by the Canadian parliament with regard to what Canada should do in the future. But that has not been accorded to us. We are going to be able to discuss this afterwards in a defence committee which the Prime Minister is quoted as saying in one of the papers might take a year to complete its work. But the decision has already been made by the government and, strangely enough, we have not heard from the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer).

This government has been talking and its members were talking during the election campaign about keeping commitments. Let us examine their record.
Within 30 days of assuming office they have already declined to keep a commitment which was made during the election campaign. Last week in the House of Commons I put the following question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcllraith), as found at page 33 of Hansard:
Does the government intend to honour the commitment made by the Prime Minister during the election campaign to retain in Winnipeg and St. James the T.C.A. overhaul and maintenance base?
The answer given by the Minister of Transport reads in part as follows:
I can find no such commitment having been made.
Subsequently in answer to a supplementary question by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles), who I am sure will pursue this subject, the Prime Minister used the following words:
[DOT]-there was no commitment in that statement in the terms put forward by the hon. member who asked the question in the first instance.
I want to draw to the attention of the house an article which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press of Saturday, March 30, just in the heat of the election campaign. The article reads as follows:
Fred Douglas, the Liberal candidate in Winnipeg South Centre, said Saturday that if a Liberal government is elected the Trans-Canada Air Lines maintenance and overhaul base will remain in greater Winnipeg. At a press conference Mr. Douglas showed a policy statement contained in a telegram from Liberal Lester Pearson. Mr. Douglas said Mr. Pearson's statement "ensures that the T.C.A. maintenance and overhaul base will continue in Winnipeg."
I do not have the time to elaborate on this matter but no doubt other members from Winnipeg will do so. I quote again from the Free Press:
The Address-Mr. Churchill
If the base moves about 1,000 employees would be affected and a gross pay packet of from $8 to $13 million.
This is of great importance to the city of Winnipeg and to individuals. The Winnipeg Tribune of May 21, commenting on the question and answer in the House of Commons, had this to say:
Questioned in the Commons on Monday, Prime Minister Lester Pearson denied that he had made any commitment to keep the overhaul base here. From the standpoint of semantics, Mr. Pearson could argue that he has made no specific pledge concerning the overhaul base. But certainly it could have been read into his election message that Mr. Pearson was prepared to fight to keep the base here. That was the conclusion made by his own candidate and no move was made to dissuade the electorate otherwise.
It is indeed regrettable that the present government should have so badly misled the residents of Winnipeg and St. James during the course of the election campaign. I call upon them to honour their commitments, expressed or implied, that were used during the election campaign to influence the voters of greater Winnipeg and to attempt to affect the vote in that city. It was understood by the people that there was a commitment.
An equally bad error was made within four days of the government assuming office. That was the callous and ruthless treatment meted out to a first world war infantryman who served in the trenches and at Pas-schendaele. I will spare the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Teillet) any comment on this matter today but I will be referring to it subsequently and I will show the complete indifference of the Prime Minister when this matter was drawn to his attention, as it was drawn to his attention by myself by cable and by telegram. He had every opportunity to take immediate action on behalf of the veterans of this country and to protect the pension commission, and he failed to do so. He wrote it off. He gave his complete and unqualified approval of the action of the Minister of Veterans Affairs. It is a subject that will be reviewed again in the House of Commons.
The other day, Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) in speaking in this debate indicated that after the election was over he had paid a visit to the United States. I was struck by this sentence of his speech that is recorded on page 249 of Hansard. He said:
I had the opportunity of speaking to a large number of United States citizens, including persons in the government service; and whether they are justified or not, United States citizens believe they won the 1963 elections in Canada and they are waiting now for the country to be delivered to them.
That is an extraordinary experience, but I think that the election campaign which ended just a few weeks ago will be recorded

The Address-Mr. Churchill in history as one in which United States interests played a larger part than at any time for at least 50 years. I think it is important to set down on the record a summary, for Canadians of the present and for the historian of the future, of some of the main factors that loomed so large during the 1963 election. A great part of the interest shown by the United States administration in Canadian affairs centered on the question of nuclear weapons. The controversy was started by a visit to Canada by General Norstad after he had vacated his command as supreme allied commander, Europe. Ostensibly he had come to bid farewell to his Canadian friends. Whether he did the same in all of the other countries of the NATO alliance has not been disclosed. His parting words to his Canadian friends were actually a sharp attack on Canada and an unexpected and unwarranted interference in Canadian affairs. That happened on January 3.
On January 12 at a Liberal association meeting in Toronto the then leader of the opposition, now the Prime Minister, executed the very difficult acrobatic feat of reversing himself while balanced on a tightrope. For several years he had proclaimed the policy of no expansion of the nuclear club and no nuclear arms for Canada.
On January 12, however, he explained his change of position, and these are his words:
The experience and information in recent months, even recent weeks, have influenced that position.
He has yet to tell us what was the experience in those recent weeks which were the weeks of the parliamentary recess in December and January. Where was he during that period? With whom did he consult? Who caused him to change his mind? He based his January 12 speech in the house on a statement made by General Norstad on January 3. These are the words he used:
These are the facts about our nuclear defence situation today. If there are any doubts about these facts, those doubts were removed the other day by a man who should know, General Norstad. the man who for years was Supreme NATO Commander.
Mr. Pierre Elliott-Trudeau, writing in the May issue of Cite Libre poses several questions that have been in the minds of many people. Here are two of them:
Do you believe it was as a tourist that General Norstad ... came to Ottawa on January 3 to demand publicly of the Canadian government that it respect Its pledge? Do you think it is by pure chance that Mr. Pearson in his speech on the 12th January rested on the authority of General Norstad?
To continue the chronological summary, I may say that the next event was the notorious press release by the department of state in Washington, issued on January 30. Then,

on February 6, the Globe and Mail carried a dispatch from Washington which referred to that press release. The article reads as follows:
Doris Fleison writing in the Washington Star says, "It could just be that some well-meaning friend here decided to give Mr. Pearson a hand. Precisely that suggestion is going the rounds with a rather important name attached."
The Chicago Sun Times of February 3 commented:
The issue is political in Canada. The American press release seemed to correspond with the position of Diefenbaker's political opposition, Liberal Leader Lester Pearson... For our part we hope Washington hasn't committed a diplomatic bay of pigs with our friends the Canadians.
Mr. Walter Lippmann in the Washington
Post wrote:
American dealings with the Canadian government have no doubt been complicated. But the crucial issue is the same one which has disrupted American relations with France and shaken the whole western alliance and has alienated the U.S. from General de Gaulle.
It was a thoughtless decision to embroil the U.S. with Ottawa in a relatively minor aspect of the great issue which is posed from Paris.
This is a quotation taken from an article reprinted in the Calgary Albertan on February 12, 1963. Then, Mr. Pierre Elliott-Trudeau poses these questions:
Do you think that it was by mistake that the State Department sent to the press, on the 30th of January, a release reinforcing Mr. Pearson's position and bluntly calling Mr. Diefenbaker a liar? Do you believe it was by pure chance that this communique furnished to the Leader of the Opposition the argument with which he literally stuffed his speech to parliament on the 31st of January? Do you believe that it was a mere coincidence that this series of events culminated in the fall of the government on the 5th of February?
There followed during the election campaign various other incidents of which I will mention only two-the Newsweek, article in February characterized by the Toronto Star as a disgraceful attack on the then prime minister, and the Buffalo radio station, WYSL, broadcasting an editorial urging its Canadian listeners to vote Liberal as recorded in the Toronto Telegram of April 4.
After the campaign came the gloating from Washington as reported in an editorial of the Globe and Mail of May 2, and a news story in the Toronto Telegram of April 24. Mr. Richard Starnes of the Scripps-Howard chain wrote as follows:
Adroit statecraft by the American State Department brought down the bungling, crypto-antiYankee government of Prime Minister John Diefenbaker and replaced it with a regime which promises to be faithful to the concept of Canadian-American interdependence ... American intervention was coldly calculated to do precisely what it did, and it was a brilliant success.

speechtext:
May I first of all congratulate the Speaker on his nomination to the high position to which he was appointed and also the Deputy Speaker and the deputy chairman of the committees. I should also like to congratulate the mover (Miss Jewett) and the seconder (Mr. Choquette) of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
It is with pride that I thank my electors of Compton-Frontenac for the confidence they have placed in me in renewing my mandate for a second time.
I can assure them that I will continue to put my humble knowledge at their service in order to fully discharge my duties as a member of parliament, which are not to be confined to patronage but should also involve all the needs and problems of my constituents in order to help those who are in need.
It is with anxiety that I listened to the speech read by the Deputy of His Excellency the Governor General.
Fine words and many flowers or rhetoric can be found in it, but I note that it is always the same kind of speech we have since confederation-a lot of meaningless words and few practical suggestions for the uplift of the

unbalanced economy facing the Canadian people and against which they have been struggling all across Canada.
I had expected to see the Liberals, for once in history, tackle the problems of the Canadian economy head on and apply beneficial and true solutions, appropriate and vital cures to the glaring economic unrest as, for instance the host of the outcasts of fortune, the homeless, the numerous unfortunate victims of the oppression of the many by the few.
The Liberals did delude those poor people and tossed them in a blanket by presenting themselves as completely new men during the last election campaign of last April 8, and pretending they had a rejuvenated party with a new spirit, strengthened by new ideas, a party with new policies, and contending that under its leadership the Canadian people would have a brand new economy and unprecedented stability.
I find that the speech from the throne is meaningless and, as I said earlier, it is almost identical to all those made since confederation, except that this time there is something new in the field of nuclear weapons. The Liberals are in orbit. They are thinking about the moon. They are getting away from earth and from worldly concerns. They know nothing about the problems of needy families, they no longer think of the unemployed. They want us to swallow the matter of nuclear weapons, they want peace, but they prepare for war.
In the Friday, November 16, 1962 issue of the Montreal daily Le Devoir, Hugh MacLen-nan stated the following:
In universities throughout the world and, I believe, even in universities behind the iron curtain, everyone agrees that an international policy based on nuclear fear must normally lead to an inconceivable disaster.
What do we of our generation want, whether we be old or young, men or women? War or peace? Life or death? If we want to live, we undoubtedly want peace.
Now, the question is, what sort of peace do we want? A confused peace, in which we shall rot away miserably, facing a hopeless future for our young people, in homes too poor to have children and to bring them up decently.
That is the sort of peace which this unsettled government offers us, whose administration deprives the poor in order to pay war debts, unemployment debts to "money makers", expenses for guns, aircraft and nuclear arms.
No, that is not the kind of peace we want, what we want is an orderly, settled peace. Peace with all the other countries, but, first

and foremost, peace among ourselves, in our own country, peace between capital and labour, between management and labour, between unemployment and technical advance, between this country's wealth and the living standard of our people. That is the peace we want. It is obvious that we know what we aim at: As much money as there are products, a constant balance between our buying power and the goods offered for consumption.
Let us have a showdown: People are dissatisfied with the present government. In this our Canada, as well as throughout the world, there is general discontent and grumbling, discontent due to constant fear, chronic insecurity, and groundless destitution. One crisis breeds another, so that, on the one hand, great quantities of essential assets and efforts are lost, while on the other hand, half the people in the world suffer from the pangs of hunger. Here, Canadians are fighting unemployment crowded and crammed in slums.
Farming is in a state of depression. Gerard Filion, the columnist of Le Devoir, wrote on November 7 last, and I quote:
The farmers are up in arms and it is serious. Political parties ought to have the problem of agricultural economy thoroughly examined once more by experts, so as to offer something else than panaceas. It is serious, because the agricultural class is entitled to a decent living.
A fact remains which nobody can deny: it is that the present economic system praised so much by the two old line parties, works badly, leads to credit restrictions, unemployment, misery and to the inconsistencies of privation amidst plenty.
It is precisely because economists of the two old line parties did not want to see the facts that they proclaimed for a long time that the Social Credit theory was a utopia. But is the present system that our economists persist in defending so consistent with reality? Has it proved so great a success? Does it bring the necessary solutions? Will they be the last and only ones to defend it?
What is so utopian in Social Credit? Is it utopia to turn our country's wealth to the benefit of our families, to put within the reach of everyone that which everyone contributes to produce?
People do not eat according to the food produced in the country; people do not dress according to the clothes manufactured in the country; people do not stay in houses according to the lumber and building materials of the country. The basic criterion remains the sum of money the system allows us.
Popes have denounced such a state of affairs, but it goes on. Every human being is
The Address-Mr. Latulippe entitled to the necessaries of life. Money must be geared to production, not production to money. Systems are made for men, not men for systems. Money must not limit human freedom and self-achievement. Here is an extract from the financial column of La Patrie signed by Marcel Ouimet on November 21, 1962, and I quote:
Any economic system is subject to continuous change, and capitalism is no exception to the rule. At the present time, the contribution made by the enterprise economy will therefore be appreciated to the extent it will succeed in enlisting every one's support, said Mr. Kierans, and in adapting itself to people's needs and in presenting itself to the still uncommitted countries as an acceptable system of social organization which can best combine material progress and complete respect for human values.
Today's economic system is based on money, and so it starts at the wrong end. Finance controls and governs production, production governs consumption, man must get along with what he is offered and what he is allowed to get. Why must our province of Quebec account alone for almost half the unemployed in Canada, or more exactly 36 per cent of them? Is our well known patience to be pushed to the limit?
In fact, a booklet entitled "Unemployment in Canada" and published by the dominion bureau of statistics under catalogue no. 71-503F, shows that between 1951 and 1955, years during which we lived under a Liberal administration, the unemployment figures by region give Quebec 36 per cent of all the unemployed in Canada. The same situation prevails during the Conservative administration between 1956 and 1960.
Our work force being only 27 per cent, a sharp difference of 35 to 40 per cent between the per capita income in Quebec and Ontario is the lot of the population in the province of Quebec.
Would not that be reason enough to provoke those poor people, forced to live in slums because they have no purchasing power, because they cannot get the money that is so cheap to produce, because, try as they may, they cannot sell the strength and production of their arms?
And injustice does not strike only the unemployed or the small wage earners in our cities. Because a great number of people lack enough purchasing power, the farmers are forced to sell their products below cost, even if they evaluate their work at only 50 cents per day.
Personally, I have come to the conclusion that there is a fifth column at work to drive the Canadians away from the system that

The Address-Mr. Latulippe prevails in Canada, to kill all ideals in their hearts and thus to hurt our economy.
You can not stand up in defence of a given regime if you do not really care for it. I feel it is high time for the authorities to pay some attention to this fifth column of ours.
Bankers reject the idea of a well-balanced economy and try to postpone its advent. They do not mind seeing people with empty pockets, and would much rather control mortgages and increase our national debt than help the state give the people wholesome and proper food and lodgings, capable of maintaining a decent army of workers and of warriors.
It is generally recognized that the family is the main cell of the national body. If we do not have a truly patriotic legislation, taking into account the elementary needs of large families, we shall see on the home front, long before enemy bombs might start falling-our families dispersed, our birth rate disrupted, our population drained of its lifeblood-and all this for what reason? In deference to figures and regulations which place money above human capital.
Hitler was blamed because of his disregard for human life. Does our tight money system have regard for human life? Has not the time come to redress and rectify a disorder which weakens our cause?
In order to support my argument, I shall quote a paragraph printed black on white on page 878 of the 1954 decennial review of the Bank Act.
At this time the chartered banks have accumulated securities of every kind, representing a total of about ten billion dollars. As strange as this may seem, they have acquired all these assets from the people and the government of Canada for practically nothing. That has been possible because, first of all, the banks have stocked up securities without spending so much as a cent. They obtained everything by resorting to trickery. It is high time that they give back their ill-acquired securities or that they be made to pay for them.
The banks are pretending that they have paid or lent ten times the amount they now hold or have collected; that they have issued money to acquire their holdings, or that they bought them with their customers' money. That is as false as can be: it is a despicable way of cheating people. This is what they really did: instead of using their own capital for constituting their holding, they simply credited their customers' accounts with the amounts owed. If those liabilities to their clients had been paid by the banks, there would have been no reason to complain. But, strange as it may seem, all was cancelled, rescinded or repudiated later on, so that the securities making up the holding remained in the hands of the banks without ever being paid for.
Why not start by paying allowances in proportion to the cost of living. I don't mean a

fortune for everybody, but at least what the humane society would ask for the average pedigreed dog. It would be less expensive and would bring in more for the nation than the interest paid to the bankers.
In view of the great dangers that have been mentioned, would it not be proper to put all our forces into the service of the nation, even the banking force. The bankers might do much better that way, because, about a week after they have been made out, all cheques come back to them perfectly safe and in good order.
Let us hope that our leaders will soon open up their eyes and bring to reason the fifth columnists supplying credit a drop at a time and paralysing the traditional family organization, promoting higher taxes, to such a point John Doe is beginning to wonder who is the boss.
Just think: the citizens choose candidates who are already selected; the politicians deceive their electors, promote political prejudice, make speeches stuffed with distortions of the truth and half truth, strive to repay their fund subscribers and faithfully serve those who have the money. I could name several of them here in this house.
Think also of the system of political patronage used to hand out the right to live for the price of degradation, abuse and delation. Think of the civil power, which should govern from above, as a sovereign and supreme judge, in all fairness and only in the interest of the common good and of justice. It has fallen to the level of a slave and has become the manageable instrument of all passions and ambitions of private interest.
The inability shown by statesmen throughout the world to solve the problems facing them is the underlying cause of crisis and wars which have been suceeding each other for several decades.
Why should the province of Quebec alone have almost half the jobless in Canada, or more precisely 36 per cent of them? Do they want to aggravate the virtue of patience which characterizes us?
If the democratic nations had succeeded in distributing the products of industry to the people, they would never have had to face the terrible threat of totalitarian states.
We, in America, are at present going through a crisis, we have to spend billions of dollars, we have to abandon our traditional occupations, and to support the staggering burden of taxatidn and indebtedness simply

because democracies did not have in the past enough social awareness to give the essentials of life to every element of the community.
They ignored the fact that if they neglected to operate the system equitably for all, they would bring about indirectly destruction of democratic capitalism.
The only thing for us to do is to take the necessary means which Social Crediters have been advocating for years and years:	a
national dividend to all members of the community, supplemented by compensated discounts.
If, after such evidence, people still want to close their eyes to reality, we repeat that the true enemies of democracy are within and the day will certainly come when public opinion will send them one by one to its merciless tribunal.
Error cannot always win over truth.
But there is in this world, no intelligent being who after having pondered the matter at any length who would not admit the truth of my repeated statements. That may have been why Henry Ford said:
If the American public knew of the corruption of their money system, there would be a revolution tomorrow morning.
The basic evil is that the leaders of all our democracies refuse to admit the current reality or do not want to realize that humanity has reached a stage in its development where productivity is so enormous that the whole system of wage payment and other similar forms of remuneration or distribution have become entirely obsolete and must make way before a system based on an accurate assessment of the facts.
Well understood Social Credit is genuine enough not to be against anything in a negative manner; it is simply for the complete truth, in order to take its place in a well balanced community.
We are wondering what the old governments have done to build up a debt-free system, a monetary system based on existing production and on production potential. What have our two old governments done to guarantee to everybody, out of our gigantic production, the vital minimum required? What pieces of legislation have they enacted in order to protect large families? What legislation have they passed to protect farmers and settlers, apart from the system of debts that we have now?
Social Crediters have been shouting for 35 years now: since the store-houses are full, it is possible to put something on the tables; since the warehouses are bulging, we can also
The Address-Mr. Webster fill the houses; since merchandises are piling up in the stores, we can put some in the homes so that each and everyone receives the share which is his through progress and science transmitted from generation to generation.
