Mr. Speaker, I wish to be associated with the congratulations and expressions of appreciation that have been extended to all presiding officers of the house during this debate. Anyone who values our parliamentary institutions must recognize the necessity of orderly procedure based on self-discipline and respect for the authority of the Speaker. The alternative is anarchy.
Since the opening days of the twenty sixth parliament I have frequently thought of two former Vancouver members with long records of service in this house. One is Angus Mac-Innis who represented Vancouver East and later Vancouver-Kingsway continuously from 1930 until 1957, and the other is Howard Green who sat for Vancouver Quadra from 1935 until 1963. Although Mr. Maclnnis is a Prince Edward Island socialist and Mr. Green a British Columbia Conservative, these gentlemen have much in common-humility, integrity, courage and dedication to the public good. I am sure that all members who knew them will join with me in wishing them good health and many happy years of retirement on the Pacific coast.
The speech from the throne reminds us of our association with the commonwealth, of the meeting of prime ministers last year and of the brief visit of our present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) to the British Isles early this month.
There have been many meetings in London since the first conference in 1887. In the beginning they were called colonial conferences, then imperial conferences and later commonwealth conferences. It is significant too that in 1887 those who attended were not even members of parliament but government officials who met under the chairmanship of the British colonial secretary. Now the prime ministers of the autonomous states meet as equals.
From 1897 until 1911 Sir Wilfrid Laurier constantly opposed the Chamberlain policy of political federation with a central parliament in London, and from 1915 until 1919 Sir Robert Borden insisted that the time had passed when the British prime minister could speak for the whole empire, and successfully urged that each dominion could be bound only by its own ministers in the imperial war cabinet, at the Versailles peace confer-

The Address-Mr. Webster ence and later at the league oi nations. Canadians should remember with gratitude the leadership of Laurier and Borden at a critical time in our national life. They spoke out frankly on behalf of this young nation. What Sir Wilfrid referred to as a "galaxy of nations under the British crown" Sir Robert described as "autonomous nations of an imperial commonwealth". Had their vision been less clear and their courage less strong, the course of this country and of the commonwealth would have been very different.
The commonwealth has no parallel in history. Centralized empires there have been, colonies there have been which have become independent states, but there have been no other instances of colonies becoming free and then turning to co-operative association with one another and with the mother country. This political evolution has been the result, not of breaking sharply with the past nor of standing by and allowing matters to drift, but of developing and extending proven institutions to fit new circumstances.
Once again the British genius for government, for adaptation and compromise, is being tested as she considers a new relationship with her neighbours on the continent of Europe. The attitudes of men all over the world are changing. A few years ago who would have thought that western Europe would be bringing itself together in a dynamic economic and political association where old traditional rivalries and state sovereignties are being submerged in a new pattern of public administration that can only be described as revolutionary? Dissolution of a centuries old empire has been accepted, even accelerated by Britain herself. So, too, all over the world we have this greater conception of human brotherhood, of a common humanity which defies our old ideas of a static world and demands a new dimension in our thinking.
In Canada only men of little faith and narrow vision fear this historic development. This must be Britain's decision. It remains for the Canadian government to respond with good grace and with energy and resourcefulness in taking advantage of new trading opportunities wherever they may appear. I have no doubt that the commonwealth will continue to grow in strength as a unique instrument for peace and progress throughout the world. To this end the Canadian government should play a leading role in improving the means of communication between the component parts of the commonwealth and in promoting co-operative measures at the world trade conference to be sponsored by the United Nations in 1964. I was pleased to read the following comment of Lord Home, British

foreign minister, in the Ottawa Citizen last week:
It is an excellent thing to see Canada playing an active part in the political councils and economic activities of the commonwealth as she approaches her centenary.
The speech from the throne implies quite correctly that the most vital question before mankind today is to learn how to live together without plotting to destroy one another, in brief, to avoid nuclear war. To this end Canadians should associate themselves with others to create a world climate that is conducive to peace everywhere. Scientists and artists do it in their areas of interest and activity, as demonstrated at the UNESCO festival in Ottawa last week. Why not politicians? We must be humble enough to adjust our attitudes to other people who may have coloured skins, speak strange tongues and worship foreign gods. We must learn to understand and trust people, all kinds of people, if we wish to survive the twentieth century.
If an individual claimed for himself the self-righteous moral values that public men and writers attribute to our nation, he would be considered beneath contempt. But to talk of the foreign policies and attitudes of our own country in anything less than superlatives which pay solemn tribute to our nobility and high moral purpose is to be unpatriotic. In very truth, according to our present standards humility and patriotism are incompatible.
When Oliver Wendell Holmes was over 80 years of age he once declared that he had spent the first 70 years of his life learning that he was not God.
In the United Nations assembly delegates speak with respect of one another in discussing the most controversial subjects. But in national parliaments like our own House of Commons we are inclined to refer in derogatory terms to countries with whom we are not aligned in the cold war. We should stop thinking in absolute terms of black and white, good and evil, slave and free.
I wish to present four witnesses who remind us that we have a responsibility to examine our own minds in relation to other people. Sydney Harris in a column last week in an Ottawa paper said this:
None of us should listen to a man giving a lecture or preaching a sermon on his philosophy of life until we know how he treats his wife, his children, his neighbours, his subordinates and his enemies.
Raymond B. Fosdick, in a recent article in the New York Times commenting on a statement of Admiral Radford's that "we cannot trust the Russians", said this:
It may be true, but that is also what the Russians profess to think of us. That is what the Athenians under Pericles said about the Spartans. It is what the Romans said about the Carthagenians. It is

what both Catholics and Protestants said about each other in the 16th century as they began a hundred years of reciprocal slaughter. It is what many modern nations have said about one another in two recent world wars. It is what the north and south charged a century ago here in the United States as they plunged into a fratricidal mania from which even today we have not fully Recovered.
My third witness is Prime Minister Harold Macmillan who, on November 6, 1962, said in the British House of Commons, and I quote:
We must not be cynical and believe nothing but ill of certain classes of our fellow men-much as we may dislike the doctrines they follow. One cannot live in a world which is just nothing but suspicion and fear or life becomes intolerable.
My next witness is U Thant, secretary general of the United Nations. In closing his acceptance speech to the assembly on November 30, 1962, he spoke very earnestly as follows:
These problems can be solved only by good will and mutual understanding and by a spirit of give and take.
When the future of mankind itself is at stake no country or interest group can afford to take a rigid stand or claim that its position is the only right one and that others must take it or leave it. No difficult problem can be solved to the complete satisfaction of all sides. We live in an imperfect world and have to accept imperfect solutions which become more acceptable as we learn to live with them and as time passes by.
The speech from the throne reminds us that Canadian unity is being threatened at the very time we are preparing to celebrate 100 years of confederation, and at the very time when we need to be strong to play our full part as a young and vigorous democracy in world affairs. In Quebec, the advocates of withdrawal from confederation repudiate 200 years of nation-building, including the glorious periods of Papineau and Mackenzie, Laurier and Borden and more recently King and St. Laurent.
Let us not forget, too, that every province has been strengthened and enriched by thousands of industrious and gifted French Canadian families who have made their homes in all sections of this country from the mari-times to British Columbia. Their contributions to Canada and their interests must be considered in any future plans designed to strengthen confederation. Ignorance on both sides is our greatest danger, a continual source of misunderstanding and irritation between English speaking and French speaking Canadians. In spite of modern means of communication and travel, Canadians in the west and Canadians in the east remain strangers in many ways. A reporter in the Globe and Mail a few days ago advised us to plan a do-it-yourself birthday party for 1967. This is an excellent suggestion. However, I would urge that we expand the idea and call it a get-acquainted party.

To this end, I recommend that we stop thinking of Canada as a melting pot. This conception of nation building is outdated, unrealistic, unimaginative and destructive of important values. We should seek unity through variety not similarity; unity through mutual appreciation, not through dull conformity; unity through justice, not through discrimination. At all costs, let us avoid becoming a nation of sheep. Mahatma Gandhi once said, "I like to think of the winds of time blowing the cultures of all lands around my doorstep".
We must build greater respect and understanding for one another in the fields of education, culture and sports, as well as commerce and industry. Exchange of language teachers at the secondary school level and of university students should be encouraged between Quebec and the western provinces. Furthermore, there should be an immediate speeding up of plans to teach the French language to more and more elementary school classes across the nation. In this connection, I recommend that all hon. members read the challenging article by Pierre Berton in the latest issue of Maclean's magazine.
A democratic society calls for a maximum development of every individual as a worker and as a citizen. No Canadian, regardless of the poverty or isolation of his home, should be neglected. In order to provide instruction and training for all who can benefit from it, governments must give high priority to school and university budgets. The local taxpayers cannot be expected to carry the major burden. The federal government should support higher education and research on a new and imaginative scale as recommended in scores of recent reports on this subject. I hope that the absence of any reference to this subject in the speech from the throne does not mean that this government contemplates a backward step in this department.
Canada will become a second-rate nation if we do not recognize education as a major social enterprise of national importance. If we do less we will make a farce of the boast that we believe in equality of opportunity for Canadian youth.
A study of biculturalism is to be commended. However, much can be done now by public spirited leaders in every community. Let us encourage the wider use of our present means of communication and travel. Let us remind our fellow Canadians that we own a Canadian broadcasting system with both radio and television in both English and French; trans-Canada railway and telegraph service; an air line, and a trans-Canada highway which permits one to motor at top speed

The Address-Mr. Webster across this nation. Let us encourage more people to use their own facilities to move east and west instead of north and south. It would be good for all of us.
Thousands of our friends go south every summer from force of habit. The same situation prevails in British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia. Let us change the direction of our holiday migrants for the good of Canada. "Let's get acquainted" should be a major objective of the centennial committee.
However, if we are to have a strong, united Canada, this parliament should be content with nothing less than full employment long before 1967. Nothing contributes more to frustration and bitterness or loss of confidence in one's country and its social system than long periods of unemployment. The relatively poor economic conditions in Quebec provide a major source of discontent among the working people and farmers in that province. To a lesser degree, this is true in all areas across the dominion.
Bold measures must be taken to expand production and distribute goods to both domestic and foreign markets on an enlarged scale. This is the challenge to those who have the responsibility for introducing and administering the various planning bills foreshadowed in the speech from the throne. Unemployment is the most outstanding weakness in our Canadian economy today. Both the public and private sectors must co-operate with the government, management and labour to develop means of working in concert towards the objective of full employment.
The Vancouver Sun, a staunch Liberal paper, in commenting on unemployment demonstrations in England said this in an editorial, and I quote:
Here in Canada few if any delegations plague our M.P.'s in the corridors of the house. Here, even in the midst of a federal election campaign, unemployment is little stressed as a major national issue.
The Englishman becomes agitated, indignant and mildly violent when less than 5 per cent of the national labour force is unemployed. Canadians, with 8 per cent of the labour force idle, show no similar trepidation.
Does this show that we are qualified to instruct the emotional Englishman in respectable restraint and political propriety? Or are we just hardened to unemployment?
Thirty years ago this July, in London, I heard a Scottish miner by the name of David Kirkwood cry out from his seat in the House of Commons, "Mr. Speaker, the work is all done". This is an exaggeration, of course. However, his remark contained an important truth which we are just beginning to appreciate in this age of automation as revealed, for instance, in many of the recommendations of the Glassco commission.

Is it true that we have become hardened to unemployment? Last Monday, after speaking for almost two hours, the leader of the official opposition made an offhand reference to unemployment. He said that one of his lieutenants would no doubt deal with the matter later in the debate. Apparently the subject was of no great importance. It would be interesting to know if the present Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) is still of the opinion that 2 per cent or 3 per cent unemployment must be expected in this country as a matter of course. In a citizen's forum debate with the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) last winter the minister, then plain Mr. Sharp, said:
I should think this is about the sort of minimum level of unemployment that is compatible with the free working of the system.
In answer to this statement Mr. Knowles remarked:
I think Mr. Sharp let the Liberal cat right out of the bag. He said the level of unemployment should be as low as is possible being compatible with the system. There is the Liberal approach-keep the system that we've got. That is more of a god than getting rid of unemployment. We say if necessary change the system to get rid of unemployment completely.
If medical scientists had accepted diphtheria, tuberculosis, small pox or diabetes as incapable of treatment, would we ever have found the means of preserving the health of countless thousands of people in the past 50 years?
If the current illness in our economy requires new procedures, new controls- "human direction" to quote Lewis Mumford -they should be undertaken in the interests of a strong, healthy, happy Canada. A few weeks ago the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) responded in a matter of hours when flood conditions in the Northwest Territories endangered the lives of our fellow citizens. We applaud him quite properly for his initiative, energy and compassion, but why do we not display the same kind of concern for the families of the half million men and women who are without work across the country? Intelligent people know that this depressed condition will be ignored at our peril.
If Canada is to be united and strong as it approaches its centennial, the government must take bold and decisive action to place legislation before us in this session that will prove effective in meeting this human tragedy.
In closing, I wish to quote a statement by the late Archbishop of Canterbury, Dr. William Temple:
If a bridge is to be built, the church may remind the engineer that it is his obligation to provide a really safe bridge but it is not entitled to tell him whether, in fact, his design meets this require-

ment. Similarly, when the church is asked to provide the Christian remedy for unemployment it must answer, 'No, I cannot tell you what is the remedy, but I can tell you that a society in which unemployment is a chronic feature is a diseased society and if you are not going to do all you can to find and administer a remedy you are guilty before God.'
I thank the house for its attention.

Mr. Speaker, may I also, in the time honoured tradition of the house, congratulate you on your appointment to the high position which you hold, and may I congratulate the Deputy Speaker on his appointment. I would also like to take this opportunity of following my colleagues on both sides of the house in congratulating both the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from throne, the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett) and the hon. member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette). May I say too that I am proud to be a member of the party which is now in government, and especially proud to be led by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson).
I am most happy and proud to have been elected by the people in my riding of Hamilton West as their representative in this house. My predecessors have represented the riding with distinction, and I pray and trust I shall follow in their footsteps. Hamilton West is composed of many diverse peoples of diverse occupations-the labourer, steelworker, small businessman, executive, industrialist and financier. Within its electoral boundaries are to be found industry, McMaster University with its nuclear reactor, the business, commercial and financial centre of the city of Hamilton, the new city hall of which all Hamiltonians are justifiably proud, and the new county court house of the county of Wentworth, which is the finest court house not only in the province of Ontario but in all of Canada at the present time. Also within its electoral boundaries is the port of Hamilton, one of the most important ports on the great lakes and St. Lawrence waterways system, and it also contains some very fine residential areas, both old and new.
In the speech from the throne there are proposals which, when translated into legislation and approved by the house, which I fully expect they will be, will be of great benefit to the people of my riding and to all other Canadians. I will not touch upon all of the proposals, as previous speakers have adequately done so. Instead I shall restrict my comments to a few, those which are of the utmost importance to my riding and the people of Hamilton generally.
The city of Hamilton is justifiably known as the "ambitious city." It is the industrial
The Address-Mr. Macaluso and steel centre of Canada. Industry is the lifeblood of this country, and the steel industry is the lifeblood of the people in Hamilton, not only of the steelworker but of those in all fields of enterprise within the city. Therefore the immediate establishment of a department of industry to foster industrial expansion and provide the many new jobs that are so badly needed, in order to check the large scale unemployment of recent years, will be anxiously looked forward to by the people in my riding.
As an alderman in the Hamilton city council for ward 2, a ward wholly situated within the electoral boundaries of Hamilton West, and which seat I will soon resign, I can say that the intention of the government to establish a municipal development and loan fund is a great step forward in the long awaited additional assistance from the federal government to the over burdened budgets of our municipalities, in order that capital projects can be commenced and completed, not only to provide and improve services but also to provide further means of employment.
My constituents in Hamilton West will be especially and particularly interested in the proposed amendments to the National Housing Act. Hamilton, as I have said, is known as the ambitious city, but it is also a gracious city. Its hand is extended in friendship to all who come there for a visit, or to make the city their home. Hamilton West has much to offer-good business opportunities, complete shopping facilities, pleasant residential areas and an excellent school system from kindergarten to postgraduate university level. However, parts of our city are getting old; some are well over 100 years old. Many of the original buildings still remain, and the street pattern has been virtually unchanged since it was first laid down.
Urban renewal and development is a reality in our city. Already there has been acquired and cleared in the Van Wagner-Crescent Beach area some 72 acres of waterfront property on lake Ontario, which consisted of blighted and low density residential homes. This area has been cleared and is presently being developed as a public park and recreational area. Further, a plan of urban renewal and redevelopment has been prepared by the city of Hamilton for the northeasterly section of my riding, encompassing an area of some six blocks, which plan has been approved by the city council and is awaiting the approval of the Ontario municipal board.
Much has been said, a great deal has been written, and not too much has been done about urban renewal in Canada. Urban renewal is a city-wide program in which all available federal, provincial, municipal and

The Address-Mr. Macaluso private resources should be applied to eliminate blight, slums, and to prevent their formation. Urban renewal has four main purposes so far in this country-clearance, redevelopment, rehabilitation and conservation.
Public acceptance of urban renewal as a concept has advanced further in the United States than in Canada, and particularly so, as it relates to assistance from the federal government. The present urban renewal program in Canada has been too narrow to cope effectively with the basic problems facing our cities. If our cities are to recapture their economic health they must offer better opportunities to commercial, industrial and residential developments and strengthen the cultural and recreational facilities of their cores.
The extent to which a federal government should be a direct participant in the financing of urban renewal is a matter which leaves room for a difference of opinion. In the United States the federal government enters into a direct contract with the municipality concerned. Under part 5 of the National Housing Act of Canada arrangements may now be made with a province or with a municipality with the approval of the province to conduct studies of the condition of housing and urban areas. Federal contributions may be up to 75 per cent of the cost of such studies. There is further provision for clearance grants in the amount of one half of the difference between the cost of clearance and the economic value of the land when cleared. The remaining 50 per cent of subsidy is financed by the province and/or the municipality as determined by the province. The important thing to note here is that clearance grants have only been made available for the purpose of clearing land which is substantially residential and which is to be redeveloped substantially in a residential form. At one time in the United States the same was true, but there has been progressive widening of use of their clearance legislation to a point that urban renewal funds may now be used for non-residential renewal projects deemed necessary for sound community development.
It is in this aspect, Mr. Speaker, that we should turn our attention to the proposed amendments to the National Housing Act, that is, in the area of providing funds for non-residential renewal projects, which is so badly lacking at the present time in our legislation; in other words, for the renewal and redevelopment of the commercial core of our cities. All in all, quite a job is being done in Hamilton, and particularly in Hamilton West, where new high-rise apartments are being erected almost monthly. This is

changing the character of the southern section of my riding from clearly a residential to a more commercial area. However, the funds provided for these projects are coming mainly from private investors. The targets of those interested in urban renewal in Hamilton are considerably higher than even the accomplishments to date.
Renewal and redevelopment of the central core of Hamilton, which is situated wholly within my riding, would have three parts, I suggest-commercial, public building and residential accommodation. With respect to commercial redevelopment and public buildings, Mr. Speaker, there is no lack in Hamilton West of vacant land in the areas suitable for those developments. All along our downtown streets we find vacant land which has been created by the demolition of obsolete buildings, demolished because these structures created rentals insufficient to pay the taxes on them and the expense of operating them. Vacant land for parking gives a better net return. Our taxation system has been an important clearance tool in the commercial but not the residential field. The city of Hamilton is concerned, as are many other municipalities, about its downtown core because it feels that development must take place in that location but finds that it does not have funds to carry on the project itself. Municipal government finds itself in the position of being obliged to finance and provide public services to a scattered population in the maximum use areas and simultaneously trying to extend public service to a scattered population in the farflung new fringe areas. Inadequate city living started the rush to the city limits and beyond to the urban fringe and the suburbs.
City living can be made as desirable and satisfying as life in the suburbs. To attain this goal, however, requires more than cleaning of backyards and of painting of houses or any aspect of the "clean up, paint up, fix up" campaigns. The problem is complex and so is also the solution. Urban renewal is a continuing process and in the final analysis it will be up to the federal government to see to it that a workable program is adopted and put into practice in the field of commercial redevelopment.
I would like to quote a few excerpts from the Hamilton Spectator of Saturday, May 25, 1963, which to a certain degree shows the extent of the problem in Hamilton and Hamilton West in the redevelopment of commercial areas. I quote from an editorial by Tom F. Mills:
Before the inferiority complex becomes too complex, it should be said that good planning has gone into the north-end urban renewal area, and much work done on it by city planners. But people who come here from out of town know what they

see and feel. Just about a year ago, William Zeckendorf, Jr., president of Webb and Knapp, Inc., leading redevelopers, made a controversial assessment: "Hamilton is in need of complete revitalization of its downtown core." Without immediate action, he said, there could be complete deterioration, and he urged efforts to have Hamilton industries build office buildings downtown.
This to date has not been very successful, Mr. Speaker. He goes on:
-we think perhaps the most significant comment about Hamilton was made here only in March by Mr. John James, planning chief for Great Britain's ministry of housing and local development.
Mr. James said, according to this article:
There is a loose fabric in Hamilton which is very odd ... I would like to see more heartbeat in the downtown area.
Mr. Mills then goes on to say:
A favourable sign is renewed talk of an auditorium and of other proposals stirring in the downtown sector; there are indications that the graph of civic spirit is rising. And of course there is more to town planning than the creation of zoning areas and the drawing of land use maps, basic as these are in a properly planned city. But we must also have the stimulus of optimistic architects' sketches of pedestrian malls, public parks and buildings downtown.
The "loose fabric" sensed by Mr. James must be drawn tight; the heartbeat made stronger so Hamilton can restore itself to a proud position among the great and progressive cities of Canada.
I do not wish to show by these comments, Mr. Speaker, that Hamilton is not progressive and is not advanced but I merely put this forward to show that the problem which exists in Hamilton also exists at this time in many of our municipalities and cities, for example, the metropolitan area of Toronto. In order to revitalize our downtown cores the federal government must take steps in moving forward with amendments to the National Housing Act to extend grants for urban renewal, not only for urban renewal in residential areas but also urban renewal in the commercial field. Urban renewal and development has another aspect in that it is more calculated to stimulate our economic recovery, provide more jobs and create further employment.
Mr. Speaker, may I call it six o'clock.

Mr. Speaker, I now join with all the other hon. members who have spoken in extending my congratulations to you on your election as Speaker. You will have the respect of every member of the house as of right, but sir, you will have an opportunity very few Speakers have had in this house, that of presiding over a committee which will consider a reform of the procedures of the house. By the manner in which you do that you can earn the highest respect of every hon. member here and of everyone in Canada.
As you preside over that committee I know you will acknowledge that this is a most able house. If the twenty fifth parliament was considered to be one of the most able we ever had, I am sure you will agree hon. gentlemen here make this one even more so. None of us sought election to this house merely for the sake of prestige, if there is any prestige left in being a member of parliament. Most of the hon. gentlemen here have been highly successful in their private careers and have received the highest of accolades from their fellowmen in their own communities. I sincerely believe we all came here to contribute our ideas, imagination, and the value of our experience to the government of our country. But, sir, do you wonder at times that there is a sense of frustration?
If a lot of hon. members had not sought election but had stayed at home and looked

after their careers, it is quite possible, in fact likely, they would be appointed to many of the commissions and boards which are formed from time to time, but being members of the house it seems to me a great part of their job boils down to a matter of voting yea or nay.
With the greatest respect, Mr. Speaker, I would like to suggest that this committee over which you will have the honour to preside should consider whether or not some of the hon. gentlemen here could be appointed as members of these boards or committees, if the powers of parliament have to be delegated to such bodies. I am sure most hon. gentlemen opposite will agree that when they occupied the government benches, they found that the distance from here to the seats of the mighty is no shorter on this side of the house than it is from any other corner of the house, and that it is sometimes difficult to express the individual talent which each member brings with him. I believe that if it is a fact that the government of Canada has to rely more and more on the senior civil service for both administration and legislation, then the committee over which you will preside should consider whether it would be a good thing for the country to merge the two powers into one.
Surely, sir, there should be some consideration given to an expansion or extension of the committee system of parliament so that hon. members could have much closer contact with various problems, and contribute more to government and to the administration? I seriously suggest that the expansion and strengthening of the committee system in the house would be beneficial to all Canadians, and would allow most hon. gentlemen here to contribute more of their talents and ideas to the government, so that the measure of a man will not be taken as his conformity or his acquiescence, but will be based on his ideas, work, talent, reputation and the courage of his convictions.
During most of the last session of the twenty fifth parliament a great deal of work went into the preparation and presentation of private members' bills, but what comes out of that? When the hour comes up for debate on private members' bills each speaker very seriously protests that he does not want to talk out the particular bill under discussion, but invariably it gets talked out. I do not say everything should be radically changed but, sir, as you preside over this committee I suggest you give some consideration to the matter of private bills.
There are many important matters in this country which are not necessarily a policy of one party or another, nor does the government

have to assume responsibility for certain matters that are raised. However surely some system, some new procedure, could be devised so that certain private bills, on approval by the government, could be debated in a free house and voted into law. I am sure that exercising our lungs between five and six o'clock every day is not the thing we ought to be doing at this time, in this century.
I agree with the sentiments expressed in the speech from the throne that we have to find new paths and assist in the strengthening of parliament. In that connection I am trying to recall a caution given by an author to a prince some 500 years ago. He said there is probably nothing more difficult to take in hand, more perilous to conduct and more uncertain of its future than to take the lead in the introduction of a new order of things, for the innovator will have as his enemies those who have done very well under the old system, and only lukewarm support from those who may do well under the new. But if you, sir, as the guiding hand of this committee are the instrument of deep, worth-while reforms you shall earn the laurels of this house and the nation.

In my maiden speech in 1958 I fully outlined the virtues and economic strength of my constituency. I shall not repeat my earlier account of the riding at this time, but would point out and emphasize most strongly that it is a constituency closely associated with our leader and strongly in support of the national development policies he adopted when he was prime minister. The constituency includes the city of Moose Jaw, a large part of the city of Regina, 48 towns and villages and a fine agricultural area of big and smaller family farms. Farmers, city and town residents, labour and business are almost equally represented. This means that
The Address-Mr. Pascoe
every action, or lack of action, by the present government will be of direct concern to one or more segments of the riding's economy. Therefore I can assure the members of the government front benches, especially the so-called inner cabinet of economic planners, that their decisions and policies will be carefully scrutinized and very carefully compared with the achievements of the former government since 1957. Those I represent know full well what was accomplished in national development in the past six years. They were not confused or misled by Liberal propaganda and a biased press, as was eastern Canada.
In 1957 just over 23 per cent of the electors of Saskatchewan voted Progressive Conservative; in 1958 the vote was 50.7 per cent Progressive Conservative; in 1962 it was 51.6 per cent, and in the April 8 vote this was increased to 53.9 per cent Progressive Conservative. So, Mr. Speaker, nearly 54 per cent of Saskatchewan voters endorsed the national development program of the Diefen-baker government and certainly will not be satisfied with anything less. However, from indications in the speech from the throne they are going to get much less from the new government.
At this point, Mr. Speaker, I must take strong exception to the words used in high Liberal circles on election night when Saskatchewan returned a full slate of 17 Progressive Conservative members. The Saskatchewan voters were called dirty dogs because they did not vote Liberal. Saskatchewan voters are not dirty dogs. I can assure the government, however, that they will be watchdogs; they will watch very carefully what the government does in the next two years, particularly the policies of what the hon. member for Mackenzie (Mr. Korchin-ski) called the two-headed Department of Agriculture. I say two years, Mr. Speaker, because there is almost bound to be an election in two years when the opposition becomes convinced that the great Liberal election promises, promises that were not included in the speech from the throne, will also be missing from the government's program. In two years the public will have time to contrast the country's economy with the 1962 record.
Other speakers have outlined Canada's economic gains, but we are going to emphasize this record again and again, Mr. Speaker, because the facts are a stinging repudiation of the apostles of gloom and doom now on the government side. As has been indicated, the gross national product in 1962 increased by 8 per cent to over $40 million. There was a trade balance of Canadian exports over

The Address-Mr. Pascoe
imports for the second year in succession. There were gains in total employment each month as compared with the same months in 1961. The total number of Canadian workers now stands at 6,660,000, an increase of 878,000 workers over the 5,782,000 employed in 1956, the last year of the former Liberal government. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, 878,000 more people are working now than were working under the Liberals in 1956.
Steel production is a good indication of economic strength. In 1962 our steel production increased by 10 per cent to almost 8 million tons, with each month's output from Canadian mills breaking the previous month's record. It has been described as the greatest year in the history of steel in Canada. These economic gains are a challenge to the new government. They are placed on record as a mark by which to measure the accomplishments this year of the Liberal regime. But they are not the only yardstick. Consumer prices were maintained by the former government at a level described by President Kennedy of the United States as the most stable in the western world. With the increase in sugar prices in the past three weeks, where will the consumer price level be in the next dominion bureau of statistics report, because these increased sugar prices affect many other prices.
Last Saturday I visited in Wakefield, Quebec, an old mill which is still operated by waterpower. It is an interesting old mill and I was pleased to learn that the government has acquired it for restoration and preservation. The miller was grinding feed concentrates for livestock. He said that the higher sugar prices and the sugar cane situation resulted in higher prices for molasses, and as a consequence prices for feed concentrates were higher. As I drew to the attention of the one Minister of Agriculture in office (Mr. Hays), that will increase the cost of livestock feeding and I think he should urge the government to do something about it. I would also draw to his attention the report in the Winnipeg paper that the government is being asked to control prices while the matter is being investigated.
Then there is the indicated increase in bread prices resulting from the removal by the government of the subsidy on whole milk to save the federal treasury $6 million. Coffee is going to cost 15 cents a cup. Rents appear to be going up. I have exactly the same accommodation I had when the last parliament closed in February, but the rent has been increased $22 a month for this session. In the space of four weeks it appears that this is going to be a high-price government.
There is another measure, Mr. Speaker, by which to judge the government a year

from now. This is a measurement of particular interest to prairie farmers whom I represent. It is the statement of the Canadian wheat board on wheat delivery quotas as at May 21. There are now 232 points on a 7-bushel quota, 259 points on an 8-bushel quota, and 929 points on 10 bushels. Farmers' wheat marketings for the 1962-63 crop year have set an all-time record of 300 million bushels as at the end of March. That is right here in the official d.b.s. report which I hold in my hand: 300 million bushels delivered by western farmers by the end of March, with four months still to go in this crop year. It will take great effort by the new government to match this wheat marketing effort. I think there might have been a better chance for this if the Canadian wheat board had been left with the Department of Agriculture, even with a two-headed department. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) in my opinion got off to a poor start on a television appearance shortly after taking over control of the wheat board when he said he did not need or want any help or advice on China wheat sales from the former minister of agriculture who is now sitting on the front benches of the official opposition. I suggest that the trade minister change his attitude towards the former minister of agriculture and accept all the help and advice he can get. We have come down here to play a positive opposition role, but this will have to change if our criticisms and advice are rejected out of hand.
The prairie farmers are worried about the possible loss of the wheat market in mainland China. Comments I have received on the situation present two views. One is that President Kennedy may have influenced the Canadian government to reduce its trade with China in line with American policy. The other is that China may reduce its purchases because of Canada's acceptance of nuclear arms. I pass on these farm views for the information of the government and particularly of the Minister of Trade and Commerce. At the risk of a curt reply such as he gave to the former minister of agriculture, I suggest that he make a public statement on the China wheat situation as soon as possible.
There is another worry Saskatchewan has, Mr. Speaker, this time over possible views of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon). In his report of the royal commission on Canada's economic prospects, the so-called Gordon report, the present Minister of Finance stated at page 172:
We would be hard to convince that Canadian agriculture as a whole is likely to benefit from the investment of large amounts of capital in monumental irrigation schemes.

If this statement can be taken to foreshadow any slowing down of work on the south Saskatchewan dam, the new government can expect terrific and immediate reaction.
That dam, started in 1958 by the Diefen-baker government, holds the key to realizing the full industrial potential of Saskatchewan. The signing of the agreement was one of the early accomplishments of the former prime minister. Completion of the dam will bring great benefit to the constituency of Moose Jaw-Lake Centre and other neighbouring constituencies in maintaining lake levels and assuring adequate domestic and industrial water supplies. So I hope the Minister of Finance has changed his earlier views on such projects and will not delay any contracts necessary for completion of the dam by 1966, the target date set by the present leader of the official opposition when he signed the agreement as prime minister.
There is concern in the west, Mr. Speaker, and I am sure there is similar concern in farming areas in other parts of Canada, regarding redistribution of constituencies. The speech from the throne merely states that a commission will be established to make the constituency changes. I hope this commission will realize that there is more involved in redistribution than boundary changes on a population basis. There is a need to assure each segment of the economy that it will have a fair representation in parliament. We know that there are more people living in the cities now and fewer on farms. City problems have increased, but so have farm problems. When population figures are considered by the redistribution committee, I suggest that there must be some form of weighted index to equalize farm and city representation. I hope to have more to say on this when legislation establishing the redistribution commission is introduced.
On this question of farm representation I join with other Saskatchewan members in objecting to the published statement by the Saskatchewan Liberal leader that a cabinet minister is being assigned to work with a sort of "shadow cabinet" of Saskatchewan Liberals back home. As I pointed out earlier, the full slate of 17 Progressive Conservative members were elected with the support of nearly 54 per cent of the voters. We were elected to represent our constituents and we intend to express their views in their interests. We hope the government will listen to our representations. I am sure we understand western views better than any Liberal shadow cabinet in Saskatchewan, especially if they include the Liberal organizer who has stated that the family farms cannot be maintained in modern agriculture. We believe they can. I have been an advocate of family farms, and
The Address-Mr. Pascoe
I am sure other hon. members have, too. I think that any farm legislation brought down by the government should bear in mind the need to preserve family farms.
There is one other item in the speech from the throne on which I should like to make a brief comment representing my personal views. It is in regard to the proposed commission on biculturalism. I agree with the statement that the bicultural character of Canada must be recognized. I agree as to the need for a basic partnership between Canadian speaking and French speaking people. I agree that the governments of the provinces must be consulted and that their views must form the basis for any commission study. As a matter of fact I consider the question could be better resolved by a dominion-provincial conference as suggested by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker) when he was prime minister than by the proposed commission, which at best could only make recommendations before final acceptance or rejection by the federal and provincial governments.
The comment I have to make is this: I wish to draw attention to the results of a Gallup poll which appeared in the Winnipeg Free Press on May 22, 1963, under the heading "Quebec Not Gloomy on Ties to Canada". The article says in part:
Although Quebec has a few angry separatists who want to secede from the rest of Canada, the people of that province are not pessimistic about feelings between themselves and English speaking Canada.
Thirty seven per cent in Quebec claim that relations between French and English speaking Canadians are better than they were five years ago.
I just wanted to put that on the record.
In conclusion, may I say that I agree with earlier speakers from this side who described the speech from the throne as a disappointing outline of what the government hopes to do-for Canada. As our leader has emphasized, it is not a question of getting the economy moving, as supporters of the government claimed during the election campaign. On the other hand a very definite responsibility rests on the government to keep the economy moving forward at the 1962 rate. Other speakers have pointed out the government's responsibility in this regard by quoting from an editorial which appeared in the Ottawa Journal. I should like to repeat the closing words of that editorial.
Let Mr. Pearson and his friends stop trying to give the impression that they took over a broken down Canadian economy. They took over a house in good order-a strong and going concern.
There is also a statement which appeared in the Letter-Review of April 29, and which, it seems to me, is deserving of being placed

The Address-Mr. Greene [DOT]on record. Referring to the economic state of this nation in 1962, the Letter-Review comments:
The increase has been steady, almost spectacular, and suggests that while further advances are desirable it is hardly optimistic to utter the thought that 'the economy should be got going again', it has not stopped for many years.
To sum up, Mr. Speaker, the 1962 achievements of the former government in national developments are on the record. We challenge the present government to match this record. They will be answerable to the public in about two years if they fail.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join previous speakers in *congratulating you	on	your	election	as
Speaker of this house. I am sure that you will fill with distinction the office that has in the past been occupied by so many distinguished men.
Mr. Speaker, I think it is amusing that we should congratulate	the	Speaker	especiallyin view of the efforts	made	to	force	thenominee to occupy	the	chair.	It	was	said
that Speakers used to be executed when they did not hand down the desired rulings. It is just like congratulating a supporter of Louis XIV who would be marched off to the guillotine. But this is how we do in this house and I wish to congratulate you, Mr. Speaker.
May I also congratulate the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I wish both of them success in their career both in the house and in the service of the public, commensurate with the brilliance of their effort.
Like everybody else, I support this part of the speech from the throne concerned with the establishment of a royal commission on biculturalism and bilingualism. There is only [DOT]one aspect of this general and positive endorsation of biculturalism which concerns me. Every politician today seems bent on vehemently supporting biculturalism. However, statements made by politicians on this subject have about the same weight and the same value as the admonishments of those who preach against sin. It is the right attitude but it does not bring results. Instead of stating at length our support of biculturalism I feel that this house should tackle the undoubtedly difficult task of establishing practical and realistic biculturalism. This cannot be done within the hour, overnight or even in the life of one legislature. However, any legislature which would devote itself in all sincerity to that task might, no doubt, set up the basis for biculturalism.
(Mr. Pascoe.]
I think it was comforting indeed to hear that part of the speech from the throne and the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), where he said that Canadians will be better able to realize that dual culture which confederation had in mind if they manage, in a general way, as a nation, to make fluent use of both the official languages of our federal state.
Minor details, like bilingual cheques, bilingual publicity slogans and claims with regard to the fair distribution of federal jobs, just stress the deficiencies in our confederation. If all Canadian citizens were bilingual, such details would be of no importance.
If, as I think, our leaders are honest and sincere when they publicly call for biculturalism, how shall we manage to get a Canadian citizen who speaks both mother tongues fluently. That is an aim which neither the tired men of our generation nor even the much younger and much more gifted ladies who sit in this house will scarcely attain or be able to hope for. Our aim should therefore be to blaze the trail, which tomorrow's truly bilingual citizens and leaders, will be able to follow.
Mr. Speaker, I think that, in spite of all we say, we still have not made the first step in that direction. Dr. Wilder Penfield, who analysed our Canadian brain so well tells us that ability to learn another language decreases very rapidly after the age of 13. It therefore seems that we should apply ourselves to give our young children under 13 the means and incentives to acquire a second language.
The methods to be employed to this end, if there are any, are very rare today. The direct method, which enables boys and girls of an age where they still have the best ability and aptitude, to acquire not only the other language but also some elements of the second culture, is the exchange of school children or pupils for one or two years, according to the needs. A timid start has been made in that direction, but, ordinarily, in the case of pupils of more advanced age, where the acquiring of a second language has become more difficult.
As far as I am concerned, I should have liked to send my eldest to Quebec to help him acquire a second culture. But at that time I could not afford it.
Now that I am in this house and that my income is higher, it would be easier.

But most Canadians do not have enough money to send their boys and girls to private schools.
Mr. Speaker, if we are sincere in what we say on that matter, I think we can play a great part right here in the field of biculturalism without infringing in any way on the constitution and this, simply by allotting federal funds for that so important and even vital objective. Evidently, it is the only way for our nation to work out true biculturalism.

I represent in this house the historic and renowned riding of Renfrew South. That riding stretches from Arnprior on the east at the junction of the mighty Ottawa and the roaring Madawaska rivers, to the newly incorporated municipality of Whitney at the gateway to Algonquin park on the west. The riding consists of people of varied ethnic origin-British, Scottish, Irish, Polish and German-and as such it is a pretty good crosssection of Canada as a whole, to such an extent that the newspaper pundits from time to time during an election campaign say that as Renfrew South goes so goes Canada. Believe me, Mr. Speaker, this is a great burden for a candidate to bear in the riding of Renfrew South.
Having so realized, I was somewhat taken aback when I came to the conclusion that I had brought this party in here on my back, and I was somewhat dismayed to hear our hon. friends opposite tell of how many hundreds of thousands and millions of dollars were available to my party in the winning of the election. As my hon. friends opposite have been so expert in finding out the state of the finances of the Liberal party, I would appreciate it very much if they would find out for me who got my share. I assure you that with the grave responsibility I have it would have been far easier to buy my way in than do it by footslogging, the way I had to do across the 130 miles of Renfrew South. Also, Mr. Speaker, having brought the Liberal party to this house on the back of Renfrew South I must say I was rather surprised when I arrived here to find that if I had been any farther back I would have been sitting in the Ottawa river.
The beautiful town of Arnprior, which is my home town, is one of the earliest settled communities of Ontario. At the centre of my riding we have the town of Renfrew, which bears the name of the county represented here by the constituencies of Renfrew South and Renfrew North. I would say this of the town of Arnprior, that, by reason of the active and vibrant municipal organization led by its former mayor, Robert M. Simpson, who brought secondary industry to our town, we
The Address-Mr. Greene have probably shared some of the fruits of the economy of Ontario.
In the town of Renfrew the employment situation at this time is very grave. By reason of the cancellation of the Avro contracts the aircraft industries there were put in a very poor plight and to this date nothing has been done to remedy that situation. Going farther west in my riding we come to the storied town of Eganville, an Irish settlement which is politically known as the home of the Maloneys. From Eganville came the Hon. Dr. Maloney who sat with distinction and honour on the opposite side of the house, his son, Arthur Maloney, who also, I am sad to state, sat on the opposite side of the house, and the late James Maloney who sat as minister of mines in the legislature at Toronto and with whom for many years I did battle on the hustings of Renfrew South. He is gone, and I wish to pay him my respects in this house at this time as a valiant, doughty warrior on the hustings of a fighting riding.
I would point out also, Mr. Speaker, that apart from these English, Scottish and Irish people we have in my riding in the township of McNabb the descendants of the original Laird McNabb who still bear proudly that Scottish name. We have in the townships of South Algoma and Gratton citizens of German descent who are now first class and have been first class citizens of Canada both in war and peace. There are families who bear names such as Verch but who still pronounce that name in the German fashion, Ferch. No better citizens are there in Canada than these people of German descent.
Going farther west in my riding we come to the lovely village of Killaloe and beautiful Brudenell where the Irish stock is still predominant but where help is again needed economically as the lumber industry has died out and nothing has come to take its place.
Moving farther west again we come to the grandiose land around Wilno, bounteous Barrys Bay and the summer paradise of Combermere. Here are wonderful people of Polish origin. These people of Polish origin were great friends of my predecessor on this side of the house, the late Dr. J. J. McCann, who held them very dearly in his heart. It has been one of the pleasant things in public life, so far as I am concerned, to come to know these smiling and happy Polish people who live in my riding of Renfrew South. I would point out, Mr. Speaker, that here we are sometimes concerned with two languages and two races in Canada. Let us not forget the Polish people, the Scottish people, the Irish people and the many other

The Address-Mr. Greene ethnic groups that go to make up this great land of ours which, along with the English and French, make Canada unique.
Now, Mr. Speaker, having gone over the geographical aspect of my constituency, I should like to point out that economic conditions in this beautiful and lovely riding are not as they should be. I have heard some of our friends from the province of Quebec referring to the economic shortcomings that exist in Quebec. They say that Quebec has not shared in the economic bounties of this country as has the province of Ontario. This is what troubles them most. I should like to assure this honourable house that Quebec is not alone in this area of drought. I heard an hon. member state that the average income in Ontario was $1,800, while the average income in Quebec was some $1,300. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that in my riding, and in particular in the west end of my riding where no secondary industry has ever located, the average income is far below that $1,300. Ontario, therefore, is not an economic utopia. There are hills in the metropolitan areas but there are valleys and swamps in the economy of Ontario as well as in other parts of Canada.
I do not ask that these mountains of economic prosperity such as exist in the metropolitan areas and in western Ontario be dragged down. We are not asking to pull anybody down from his lofty pinnacle. However, we do believe that those economic quagmires which exist in areas such as the west end of south Renfrew should be drained a little. We should fill in those hollows a little bit, so that my people will share in the bounties of this very rich province. I assure you that while we profess so often and so loudly that there is equality of opportunity in this land, a boy or a girl from the south end of Renfrew does not have the same opportunity for advancement, for education and for prosperity in the future, as does a boy or girl from one of the metropolitan areas. I know of many cases where boys and girls just could not go to high school because there was no high school. There was no economic foundation on which a high school could be built. The only way they could go to high school was by taxicab some 10 or 15 miles, if their mother or father could pay for it, and this in an area where there was no industry in which the mother or father could get a job to take care of this expense.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that one of the great tasks before this house is to assure that there will be equalization in this wealthy land. I believe that the spirit of the Pearson plan, as envisaged in this speech from the

throne, is that we will not add to these growing cities, these new abodes of the cave-dwellers who are more and more residing in apartment houses in the great metropolitan area. Surely, it is inherent in the speech from the throne that the economic powers of the government should be used for social purposes. What finer social purpose is there than the diversification of industry in order to enable our people to live where there are green hills, fresh air and lakes, beauty and sunshine? This would avoid the continued growth of the cities as has occurred in the past few years.
If I am correct, Mr. Speaker, in interpreting the speech from the throne in this light, then I know of no place where the diversification of industry is so badly needed, I know of no area in which industry may be located to better advantage so that the people will enjoy a better way of life, than in my own riding of Renfrew South, particularly the west end of that riding.
The whip on this side of the house, Mr. Speaker, has very kindly given priority to the new members on this side of the house in this debate. As a result of this, my colleague from Renfrew North (Mr. Forgie) may not have an opportunity to speak. With this in mind, I should like to state that I shall at all times support him in his endeavours on behalf of the town of Pembroke and the surrounding area where the problems are similar to those in my riding, since it is in the other half of the county of Renfrew. I shall be very pleased also, and proud, to support him in his continuing efforts, by which he has distinguished himself in the past, on behalf of the armed forces at Camp Petawawa. I wish to align myself, as I know the hon. member for Renfrew North has many times before, with the proposition that these men and women serving in our armed forces should receive comparable emoluments to those received by people in comparable jobs in civilian life. Without these men and women, our country would soon grow weak and the very things for which we profess to stand would be but a farce.
There is one other group of people I should like to support in conjunction with my hon. friend from Renfrew North. I refer to the employees at Deep River who are engaged in atomic research and production in Canada. We have lost too many of our most able men, of our best trained technicians, because apparently in this land we do not appreciate the contribution these people are able to make to the future of Canada. I believe that in the future we should look after these

people as best we can so that the scientific age, the atomic age, will in fact belong to Canada.
On the broader national aspect of the measures contained in the speech from the throne, I shall say very little. Other speakers from this side of the house, much better informed, much more knowledgeable and experienced than I, have gone over the variety of commitments contained in this document. I support them to the hilt in their stand on the measures therein contained. Hon. gentlemen opposite have, however, raised one point with which I shall deal briefly, namely the fear that by reason of the measures contained in the speech from the throne which involve a new use of the executive power for social purposes, there will be lost that freedom of the individual which is the very nub of our system, as compared to those systems which use control but which forego that freedom of the individual. I was very pleased, therefore, Mr. Speaker, to see that passage in the speech from the throne with regard to the committee on procedure. It clearly indicates that this side of the house is just as concerned with the rights of the individual, which are inherent in the supremacy of parliament, as are our friends on the opposite side of the house. They have attempted to perpetuate and promulgate the myth that in their own fashion they are the champions of parliament and the champions of the supremacy of parliament, but I do not believe this is the case. That the committee on procedure is to be set up is witness to the fact that this side of the house is just as concerned in this regard as any other hon. members of the house.
I may make a suggestion in a very humble fashion as a new member, Mr. Speaker, that this house can only be as strong as its individual members, and I have found in the very short time I have been here that the facilities given to the ordinary hon. member make it very difficult for him to carry out his job. We have been given horse and buggy tools in a jet age. If a man is doing the important job of representing some 30,000 to 60,000 people, and is doing that job conscientiously, then he must have far better facilities than are given to the ordinary member here.
I do not wish to appear as a precocious member, Mr. Speaker. I know I have a great deal to learn but I do think that every hon. member should at least be given a private office, with separate quarters for his staff. I do believe every hon. member should at least be given stenographic help, not just during the session but during his entire tenure, at Ottawa or in his constituency as
The Address-Mr. Greene he deems advisable. The people of Canada would be shocked if they knew the limited facilities given to their representatives in their job of representing them here in Ottawa, and I hope the house will take it under advisement, and that hon. members on the front benches on this side will give consideration to providing better equipment and better tools.
I found that even a dictaphone was something foreign to the office of a private member, and in the twentieth century surely this is something to be deplored. We have heard a great deal of talk that being a member of the house is a full time job. In the little I have seen of it, it is more than a full time job, and if we are going to do a full time job, we should have the facilities, the equipment and the help to do an adequate full time job. If we are ever going to discuss the matter of raising the emoluments of hon. members, then let us be sure we are in a position to do an adequate, 100 per cent full time job for our constituents, and that means we must have the necessary tools.
In conclusion I wish to say I am sure the measures which will be brought forth in the committee on procedure will ensure the continuing supremacy of parliament over the executive and administrative areas of government. To me the great challenge of today is this: can free peoples use the power, controls and direction which are necessary to provide full employment, and at the same time retain that freedom and supremacy of the individual which we deem essential?
I think it is correct to state that in any community or any country where the supremacy of the legislature has been subjugated, then that supremacy of the individual has been lost, from the days of the Star Chamber to the Bundestag and the Kremlin. Only if we maintain the supremacy of this house over all elements of government is the sanctity of the individual on the best and surest foundation.
I do not know how long I will be a member of the house, because in my riding it is mighty tough to stay an elected representative. Political longevity however is not my only aspiration. I hope to do something of benefit for my people and for the country while I am here, whether it be for two years as my hon. friend opposite has stated, or for 22 years; and may I say it is my fondest hope that my political epitaph, whenever it is written, will say "he served well in the House of Commons", because I believe that is the greatest challenge of our times.

The Address-Mr. H. M. Horner

Mr. Speaker, it may be only just and right that I should follow the hon. member who has spoken so eloquently on behalf of the constituency of Renfrew South. I do not agree with all he said but I certainly appreciate the very eloquent manner in which he said it. My forefathers came from the Ottawa valley and I may say I can appreciate the natural ability and oratory he acquired from his Irish ancestors in that area.
As I have said, I cannot agree with all he said. Certainly when he talked so glowingly about the speech from the throne, he must have had his hand in his pocket. There was nothing in it. We heard all the promises of the Liberal party, but where are they now? I shall deal with them one by one, but prior to doing that I want to congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, on your elevation to the speakership. I also want to congratulate the Deputy Speaker on his appointment, and the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne.
Now I wish to deal with the nub of the problem in Canada today, as I see it. There are several problems which are facing us as Canadians, but the most important one depends on whether or not we remain a country. I do not subscribe to the bumbling aspirations of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer). I do not subscribe to the bumbling aspirations of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and I want to say why, and say it clearly.
With regard first to the question of bi-culturalism I want to say this sincerely and put it on the line. I represent 2,000 French Canadians, people who took their courage in their hands and migrated to Alberta where they homesteaded. I represent these people not only in fact but by their votes. What is their message to this house, to Quebec and to Canada? Their message is simply this, that we must have a Canada first; that we want to maintain our culture but we have to have a Canada.
What about our culture? What about this thing called culture that the C.B.C. on occasion tries to shove down our throats? You do not develop culture because a minister says this, that, or something else. You develop culture by living a life, by your family living a life, and by creating and doing things different in this country, with the help of what your forefathers gave you. There is a lot of nonsense about this, and I shall speak about the press in that regard in a moment. We develop culture as we work, build and develop a country. We do not develop a culture because of United States influence. If we do, we are not a country. If this culture that we


are trying to develop and if this country that we are trying to develop does not take into cognizance this essential fact, then we are not a country. If the Liberal party persists in accepting United States money to run their campaigns-

I know that my time is limited, Mr. Speaker, but I want to say a word with regard to some of my friends in the press gallery. I have nothing to hide, nothing to be afraid of them for. to say this outside the house in any court of law. They have not reported the facts. I would like my friends in the government now to say what kind of a deal they have made with the Southam Press. I say to the people in the government, have you an agreement with the Southam Press? Are these people United States controlled? Are these people going to get a big deal out of your government? subtopic: PINAL COMMUNIQUE OF NATO MINISTERIAL MEETING

speechtext:
The north Atlantic council met in ministerial session in Ottawa from 22nd to 24th May, 1963.
2.	In their review of the international situation, ministers emphasized that in the world of today peace is indivisible. The enduring character of the north Atlantic alliance, founded on the principles of interdependence and common defence, constitutes a basic guarantee for the maintenance of peace.
3.	The council noted with regret that the Soviet union had so far shown little interest in seeking equitable solutions for outstanding problems.
4.	With regard to Germany and Berlin, the threat has not disappeared. Thanks to the firm attitude maintained by the west, however, developments detrimental to the interests of Berlin and the alliance have been effectively discouraged. In this connection, the alliance abides by the terms of its declaration of 16th December, 1958, on Berlin.
5.	Outside the treaty area too, tensions and difficulties continue to exist which have a profound effect on the alliance. Soviet military personnel remain in Cuba; and the situation there, with its repercussions in the region generally, still gives cause for concern. Ministers also expressed their disquiet over recent events in Laos, and stressed the importance of sustained efforts to secure respect for the Geneva agreements.
6.	Ministers reaffirmed the importance, in building a peaceful world, of progress toward general and complete disarmament by stages and under effective international control. In this connection, they noted that agreement in principle had been reached between the United States and the U.S.S.R. on measures to improve communications designed to reduce the risk of war by accident or miscalculation. They expressed the hope that the Soviet union's attitude would evolve sufficiently to permit genuine progress to be made on key disarmament questions.
7.	The growing scope and complexity of the problems facing the alliance make it imperative for the council to ensure that its political consultations are as prompt and effective as they can be made. Ministers noted the progress already achieved in this direction and expressed their determination to secure still further improvements.
8.	Ministers discussed NATO defence policy and approved the steps taken to organize the nuclear forces assigned or to be assigned to the supreme allied commander Europe (SACEUR).
These include notably:
(a)	assignment of the United Kingdom V-bomber force and three U.S. Polaris submarines to SACEUR;
(b)	establishment by SACEUR on his staff of a deputy responsible to him for nuclear affairs;
(c)	arrangements for broader participation by officers of NATO member countries in nuclear activities in allied command Europe and in co-ordination of operational planning at Omaha;
(d)	fuller information to national authorities, both political and military.
Ministers welcomed these measures to increase the effectiveness of the nuclear capability at the disposal of the alliance and to improve co-ordination and control of its nuclear deterrent forces.
9.	Ministers recognized the need to achieve a satisfactory balance between nuclear and conventional arms. They directed the council in permanent session to undertake, with the advice of the NATO military authorities, further studies of the interrelated questions of strategy, force requirements and the resources available to meet them.
10.	The council noted progress made in the implementation of earlier resolutions concerning the defence problems of Greece and reaffirmed its interest in the effective application of these resolutions.
11.	The north Atlantic alliance seeks peace. It deplores the diversion into the military field of resources which might be used for the betterment of mankind, and in particular for increased efforts to raise living standards in developing countries. But the free world remains faced with a continuing threat and the members of the north Atlantic alliance have both the right and the duty to protect their freedom and independence.
12.	The next ministerial meeting will be held in Paris in December 1963.
Tuesday, May 28, 1963
